a,b$}\mathclose{}{)}},q:\mathsf{path}_{\_.\mathsf{el}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle\hat{A}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle\hat{A}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\hat{A}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\hat{A}$}\mathclose{}{)}}}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle a,b$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle a,b$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle a,b$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle a,b$}\mathclose{}{)}}$}\mathclose{}{)}}
; we may
derive
\Gamma\vdash p=q:\mathsf{path}_{\_.\mathsf{el}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle\hat{A}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle\hat{A}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\hat{A}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\hat{A}$}\mathclose{}{)}}}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle a,b$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle a,b$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle a,b$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle a,b$}\mathclose{}{)}}
as follows:

boundary separation

\Gamma,i:\mathbb{I},\partial\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle i$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle i$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle i$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle i$}\mathclose{}{)}}\vdash\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\displaystyle i=\mathsf{0}\to a\mid i=\mathsf{1}\to b$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\textstyle i=\mathsf{0}\to a\mid i=\mathsf{1}\to b$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\scriptstyle i=\mathsf{0}\to a\mid i=\mathsf{1}\to b$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle i=\mathsf{0}\to a\mid i=\mathsf{1}\to b$}\mathclose{}{]}}=\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\displaystyle i=\mathsf{0}\to a\mid i=\mathsf{1}\to b$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\textstyle i=\mathsf{0}\to a\mid i=\mathsf{1}\to b$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\scriptstyle i=\mathsf{0}\to a\mid i=\mathsf{1}\to b$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle i=\mathsf{0}\to a\mid i=\mathsf{1}\to b$}\mathclose{}{]}}\in\hat{A}

\Gamma,i:\mathbb{I},\partial\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle i$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle i$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle i$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle i$}\mathclose{}{)}}\vdash\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\displaystyle i=\mathsf{0}\to p(i)\mid i=\mathsf{1}\to p(i)$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\textstyle i=\mathsf{0}\to p(i)\mid i=\mathsf{1}\to p(i)$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\scriptstyle i=\mathsf{0}\to p(i)\mid i=\mathsf{1}\to p(i)$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle i=\mathsf{0}\to p(i)\mid i=\mathsf{1}\to p(i)$}\mathclose{}{]}}=\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\displaystyle i=\mathsf{0}\to q(i)\mid i=\mathsf{1}\to q(i)$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\textstyle i=\mathsf{0}\to q(i)\mid i=\mathsf{1}\to q(i)$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\scriptstyle i=\mathsf{0}\to q(i)\mid i=\mathsf{1}\to q(i)$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle i=\mathsf{0}\to q(i)\mid i=\mathsf{1}\to q(i)$}\mathclose{}{]}}\in\hat{A}

\Gamma,i:\mathbb{I},\partial\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle i$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle i$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle i$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle i$}\mathclose{}{)}}\vdash p(i)=q(i)\in\hat{A}

\Gamma,i:\mathbb{I}\vdash p(i)=q(i)\in\hat{A}

\Gamma\vdash\lambda i.p(i)=\lambda i.q(i):\mathsf{path}_{\_.\mathsf{el}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle\hat{A}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle\hat{A}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\hat{A}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\hat{A}$}\mathclose{}{)}}}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle a,b$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle a,b$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle a,b$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle a,b$}\mathclose{}{)}}

\Gamma\vdash p=q:\mathsf{path}_{\_.\mathsf{el}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle\hat{A}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle\hat{A}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\hat{A}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\hat{A}$}\mathclose{}{)}}}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle a,b$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle a,b$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle a,b$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle a,b$}\mathclose{}{)}}

2.3.2.
Coercion and composition

Another important aspect of Bishop sets in XTT is that they support

coercion
and
composition
operations:

\hskip-6.99997pt\begin{array}[]{*{\l_matrix_num_cols}{l}}\Gamma,i:\mathbb{I}\vdash\hat{A}:\mathsf{set}&\Gamma\vdash a\in\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\displaystyle r/i$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\textstyle r/i$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\scriptstyle r/i$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle r/i$}\mathclose{}{]}}\hat{A}\end{array}\hskip-6.99997pt
\hskip-6.99997pt\begin{array}[]{*{\l_matrix_num_cols}{l}}\Gamma\vdash\mathsf{coe}^{r\rightsquigarrow r^{\prime}}_{i.\hat{A}}\,a\in\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\displaystyle r^{\prime}/i$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\textstyle r^{\prime}/i$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\scriptstyle r^{\prime}/i$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle r^{\prime}/i$}\mathclose{}{]}}\hat{A}\ \mathchoice{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\displaystyle r^{\prime}=r\to a$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\textstyle r^{\prime}=r\to a$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\scriptstyle r^{\prime}=r\to a$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle r^{\prime}=r\to a$}\mathclose{}{]}}\end{array}\hskip-6.99997pt

\hskip-6.99997pt\begin{array}[]{*{\l_matrix_num_cols}{l}}\Gamma,i:\mathbb{I}\vdash\hat{A}:\mathsf{set}&\Gamma,i:\mathbb{I},i=r\lor\partial\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle s$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle s$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle s$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle s$}\mathclose{}{)}}\vdash a\in\hat{A}\end{array}\hskip-6.99997pt
\hskip-6.99997pt\begin{array}[]{*{\l_matrix_num_cols}{l}}\Gamma\vdash\mathsf{com}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\displaystyle s$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\textstyle s$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\scriptstyle s$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle s$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}^{r\rightsquigarrow r^{\prime}}_{i.\hat{A}}{\,i.a}\in\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\displaystyle r^{\prime}/i$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\textstyle r^{\prime}/i$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\scriptstyle r^{\prime}/i$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle r^{\prime}/i$}\mathclose{}{]}}\hat{A}\ \mathchoice{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\displaystyle r^{\prime}=r\lor\partial\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle s$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle s$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle s$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle s$}\mathclose{}{)}}\to\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\displaystyle r^{\prime}/i$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\textstyle r^{\prime}/i$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\scriptstyle r^{\prime}/i$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle r^{\prime}/i$}\mathclose{}{]}}a$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\textstyle r^{\prime}=r\lor\partial\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle s$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle s$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle s$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle s$}\mathclose{}{)}}\to\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\displaystyle r^{\prime}/i$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\textstyle r^{\prime}/i$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\scriptstyle r^{\prime}/i$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle r^{\prime}/i$}\mathclose{}{]}}a$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\scriptstyle r^{\prime}=r\lor\partial\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle s$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle s$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle s$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle s$}\mathclose{}{)}}\to\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\displaystyle r^{\prime}/i$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\textstyle r^{\prime}/i$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\scriptstyle r^{\prime}/i$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle r^{\prime}/i$}\mathclose{}{]}}a$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle r^{\prime}=r\lor\partial\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle s$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle s$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle s$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle s$}\mathclose{}{)}}\to\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\displaystyle r^{\prime}/i$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\textstyle r^{\prime}/i$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\scriptstyle r^{\prime}/i$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle r^{\prime}/i$}\mathclose{}{]}}a$}\mathclose{}{]}}\end{array}\hskip-6.99997pt

In essence, these operations implement the action of paths in every set,
simultaneously enabling coercions between equal types, as well providing a way
to compose and invert paths. The coercion operation above allows, in
particular, an element of a set to be transformed into an element of any equal
set: this is the action of
\mathsf{coe}^{\mathsf{0}\rightsquigarrow\mathsf{1}}_{i.\hat{A}}\,a
. In Observational Type
Theory, there is an additional
coherence
operation that
(heterogeneously) equates
a
with its coercion
\mathsf{coe}^{\mathsf{0}\rightsquigarrow\mathsf{1}}_{i.\hat{A}}\,a
;
in XTT (and Cartesian cubical type theories generally), this is accomplished
using another instance of the general coercion operator called a “filler”:

\mathchoice{\mathopen{\mathchoice{\big(}{\big(}{\big(}{(}}\hbox{$\displaystyle\lambda i.\mathsf{coe}^{\mathsf{0}\rightsquigarrow i}_{i.\hat{A}}\,a$}\mathclose{\mathchoice{\big)}{\big)}{\big)}{)}}}{\mathopen{\mathchoice{\big(}{\big(}{\big(}{(}}\hbox{$\textstyle\lambda i.\mathsf{coe}^{\mathsf{0}\rightsquigarrow i}_{i.\hat{A}}\,a$}\mathclose{\mathchoice{\big)}{\big)}{\big)}{)}}}{\mathopen{\mathchoice{\big(}{\big(}{\big(}{(}}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\lambda i.\mathsf{coe}^{\mathsf{0}\rightsquigarrow i}_{i.\hat{A}}\,a$}\mathclose{\mathchoice{\big)}{\big)}{\big)}{)}}}{\mathopen{\mathchoice{\big(}{\big(}{\big(}{(}}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\lambda i.\mathsf{coe}^{\mathsf{0}\rightsquigarrow i}_{i.\hat{A}}\,a$}\mathclose{\mathchoice{\big)}{\big)}{\big)}{)}}}:\mathsf{path}_{i.\mathsf{el}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle\hat{A}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle\hat{A}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\hat{A}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\hat{A}$}\mathclose{}{)}}}\mathchoice{\mathopen{\mathchoice{\big(}{\big(}{\big(}{(}}\hbox{$\displaystyle a,\mathsf{coe}^{0\rightsquigarrow 1}_{i.\hat{A}}\,a$}\mathclose{\mathchoice{\big)}{\big)}{\big)}{)}}}{\mathopen{\mathchoice{\big(}{\big(}{\big(}{(}}\hbox{$\textstyle a,\mathsf{coe}^{0\rightsquigarrow 1}_{i.\hat{A}}\,a$}\mathclose{\mathchoice{\big)}{\big)}{\big)}{)}}}{\mathopen{\mathchoice{\big(}{\big(}{\big(}{(}}\hbox{$\scriptstyle a,\mathsf{coe}^{0\rightsquigarrow 1}_{i.\hat{A}}\,a$}\mathclose{\mathchoice{\big)}{\big)}{\big)}{)}}}{\mathopen{\mathchoice{\big(}{\big(}{\big(}{(}}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle a,\mathsf{coe}^{0\rightsquigarrow 1}_{i.\hat{A}}\,a$}\mathclose{\mathchoice{\big)}{\big)}{\big)}{)}}}

Composition is analogous to coercion, except that it may additionally constrain
the result to match a partial element defined on a boundary
\partial\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle s$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle s$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle s$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle s$}\mathclose{}{)}}
for some

s:\mathbb{I}
. (Because of boundary separation and regularity, XTT’s composition
operator is substantially simpler than those of other cubical type theories,
which consider partial elements defined on arbitrary
\phi:\mathbb{F}
.) Composition
can be used to define combinators expressing the symmetry and transitivity of
equality, as well as to implement Martin-Löf’s
\mathsf{J}
eliminator. In fact,
to express symmetry and transitivity, it suffices to first consider the case
where
\hat{A}
doesn’t depend on
i
, called
homogeneous composition
:

\mathsf{hcom}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\displaystyle s$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\textstyle s$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\scriptstyle s$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle s$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}^{r\rightsquigarrow r^{\prime}}_{\hat{A}}{\,i.a}\overset{\textit{def}}{=\joinrel=}\mathsf{com}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\displaystyle s$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\textstyle s$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\scriptstyle s$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle s$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}^{r\rightsquigarrow r^{\prime}}_{\_.\hat{A}}{\,i.a}

{exa}

[Symmetry]
Let
\hat{A}:\mathsf{set}
and let
a,b\in\hat{A}
and let

p:\mathsf{path}_{\_.\mathsf{el}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle\hat{A}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle\hat{A}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\hat{A}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\hat{A}$}\mathclose{}{)}}}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle a,b$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle a,b$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle a,b$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle a,b$}\mathclose{}{)}}
. We may use homogeneous composition to
define an inverse path
\bar{p}:\mathsf{path}_{\_.\mathsf{el}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle\hat{A}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle\hat{A}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\hat{A}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\hat{A}$}\mathclose{}{)}}}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle b,a$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle b,a$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle b,a$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle b,a$}\mathclose{}{)}}
:

\bar{p}\overset{\textit{def}}{=\joinrel=}\lambda i.\mathsf{hcom}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\displaystyle i$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\textstyle i$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\scriptstyle i$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle i$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}^{\mathsf{0}\rightsquigarrow\mathsf{1}}_{\hat{A}}{\,j.\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\displaystyle j=\mathsf{0}\lor i=\mathsf{1}\to p(\mathsf{0})\mid i=\mathsf{0}\to p(j)$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\textstyle j=\mathsf{0}\lor i=\mathsf{1}\to p(\mathsf{0})\mid i=\mathsf{0}\to p(j)$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\scriptstyle j=\mathsf{0}\lor i=\mathsf{1}\to p(\mathsf{0})\mid i=\mathsf{0}\to p(j)$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle j=\mathsf{0}\lor i=\mathsf{1}\to p(\mathsf{0})\mid i=\mathsf{0}\to p(j)$}\mathclose{}{]}}}\qed

{exa}

[Transitivity]
Let
\hat{A}:\mathsf{set}
and let
a,b,c\in\hat{A}
and let

p:\mathsf{path}_{\_.\mathsf{el}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle\hat{A}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle\hat{A}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\hat{A}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\hat{A}$}\mathclose{}{)}}}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle a,b$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle a,b$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle a,b$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle a,b$}\mathclose{}{)}},q:\mathsf{path}_{\_.\mathsf{el}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle\hat{A}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle\hat{A}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\hat{A}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\hat{A}$}\mathclose{}{)}}}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle b,c$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle b,c$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle b,c$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle b,c$}\mathclose{}{)}}
. We
may use homogeneous composition to define a composite path
p\cdot q:\mathsf{path}_{\_.\mathsf{el}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle\hat{A}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle\hat{A}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\hat{A}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\hat{A}$}\mathclose{}{)}}}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle a,c$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle a,c$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle a,c$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle a,c$}\mathclose{}{)}}
:

p\cdot q\overset{\textit{def}}{=\joinrel=}\lambda i.\mathsf{hcom}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\displaystyle i$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\textstyle i$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\scriptstyle i$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle i$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}^{\mathsf{0}\rightsquigarrow\mathsf{1}}_{\hat{A}}{\,j.\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\displaystyle j=\mathsf{0}\lor i=\mathsf{0}\to p(i)\mid i=\mathsf{1}\to q(j)$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\textstyle j=\mathsf{0}\lor i=\mathsf{0}\to p(i)\mid i=\mathsf{1}\to q(j)$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\scriptstyle j=\mathsf{0}\lor i=\mathsf{0}\to p(i)\mid i=\mathsf{1}\to q(j)$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle j=\mathsf{0}\lor i=\mathsf{0}\to p(i)\mid i=\mathsf{1}\to q(j)$}\mathclose{}{]}}}\qed

Remark 2
.

By boundary separation, the symmetry and transitivity operators act very strictly. For instance,
given
p:\mathsf{path}_{i.A}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle a,b$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle a,b$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle a,b$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle a,b$}\mathclose{}{)}}
one has
\bar{p}\cdot p=(\lambda i.b)

definitionally. Similarly, composition of paths is definitionally associative:

p\cdot\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle q\cdot w$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle q\cdot w$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle q\cdot w$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle q\cdot w$}\mathclose{}{)}}=\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle p\cdot q$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle p\cdot q$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle p\cdot q$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle p\cdot q$}\mathclose{}{)}}\cdot w
. In the absence of boundary separation, these
coherences would hold up to another path, using a more complex instance of the composition
operation.
∎

{exa}

[Identity type]
Using composition, we may define a combinator with
the same type as Martin-Löf’s
\mathsf{J}
eliminator for the identity type.
Let
\hat{A}:\mathsf{set}
be a set and

x\in\hat{A},y\in\hat{A},z:\mathsf{path}_{\_.\mathsf{el}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle\hat{A}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle\hat{A}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\hat{A}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\hat{A}$}\mathclose{}{)}}}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle x,y$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle x,y$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle x,y$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle x,y$}\mathclose{}{)}}\vdash\hat{C}(x,y,z):\mathsf{set}
be a motive of induction.
Fixing
a,b\in\hat{A}
and

and

x:A\vdash c(x)\in\hat{C}(x,x,\lambda\_.x)

\mathsf{J}_{\hat{C}}(p,c)\in\hat{C}(a,b,p)

i=\mathsf{0}\to p(0)\mid i=\mathsf{1}\to p(k)$}\mathclose{}{]}}}$}\mathclose{\mathchoice{\big)}{\big)}{\big)}{)}}}{\mathopen{\mathchoice{\big(}{\big(}{\big(}{(}}\hbox{$\textstyle p(0),p(i),\lambda j.\mathsf{hcom}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\displaystyle i$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\textstyle i$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\scriptstyle i$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle i$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}^{0\rightsquigarrow j}_{\hat{A}}{\,k.\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\displaystyle k=\mathsf{0}\lor i=\mathsf{0}\to p(0)\mid i=\mathsf{1}\to p(k)$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\textstyle k=\mathsf{0}\lor i=\mathsf{0}\to p(0)\mid i=\mathsf{1}\to p(k)$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\scriptstyle k=\mathsf{0}\lor i=\mathsf{0}\to p(0)\mid i=\mathsf{1}\to p(k)$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle k=\mathsf{0}\lor i=\mathsf{0}\to p(0)\mid i=\mathsf{1}\to p(k)$}\mathclose{}{]}}}$}\mathclose{\mathchoice{\big)}{\big)}{\big)}{)}}}{\mathopen{\mathchoice{\big(}{\big(}{\big(}{(}}\hbox{$\scriptstyle p(0),p(i),\lambda on a

\lambda\_.a:\mathsf{path}_{\_.\mathsf{el}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle\hat{A}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle\hat{A}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\hat{A}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\hat{A}$}\mathclose{}{)}}}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle a,a$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle a,a$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle a,a$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle a,a$}\mathclose{}{)}}
? From Martin-Löf type
theory, we would expect
\mathsf{J}_{\hat{C}}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle\lambda\_.a,c$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle\lambda\_.a,c$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\lambda\_.a,c$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\lambda\_.a,c$}\mathclose{}{)}}
to compute to

coercion regularity

\hskip-6.99997pt\begin{array}[]{*{\l_matrix_num_cols}{l}}\Gamma,i:\mathbb{I},j:\mathbb{I}\vdash\hat{A}=\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\displaystyle j/i$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\textstyle j/i$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\scriptstyle j/i$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle j/i$}\mathclose{}{]}}\hat{A}:\mathsf{set}\end{array}\hskip-6.99997pt
\hskip-6.99997pt\begin{array}[]{*{\l_matrix_num_cols}{l}}\Gamma\vdash\mathsf{coe}^{r\rightsquigarrow r^{\prime}}_{i.\hat{A}}\,a=a\in\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\displaystyle r^{\prime}/i$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\textstyle r^{\prime}/i$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\scriptstyle r^{\prime}/i$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle r^{\prime}/i$}\mathclose{}{]}}\hat{A}\end{array}\hskip-6.99997pt

Remark 3
.

2.3.4.
Algorithmic type checking and type-case

Although a type checking algorithm for XTT is beyond the scope of this paper,
such an algorithm is important to fully substantiate our claim that XTT can act
as a more tractable alternative to extensional type theory. As a step towards
applying existing type checking algorithms to XTT, we include one final construct.

Most type checking algorithms going back to the work of
Coquand
[
Coq96
]
check
M:A
by first evaluating
A
to a weak-head
normal form, in order to determine whether
A
is a dependent product type, a
dependent sum type, the booleans,
etc
. Such a determination is crucial because
the head constructor of
A
, in turn, determines how to type check
M
(
e.g
.
, by
applying it to an argument, considering its projections,
etc
.
).

Consider the case that we have a variable
x:\mathsf{path}_{\_.\mathsf{set}}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle\hat{A}\mathbin{\hat{\times}}\hat{B},\hat{C}\mathbin{\hat{\times}}\hat{D}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle\hat{A}\mathbin{\hat{\times}}\hat{B},\hat{C}\mathbin{\hat{\times}}\hat{D}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\hat{A}\mathbin{\hat{\times}}\hat{B},\hat{C}\mathbin{\hat{\times}}\hat{D}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\hat{A}\mathbin{\hat{\times}}\hat{B},\hat{C}\mathbin{\hat{\times}}\hat{D}$}\mathclose{}{)}}

in scope, and we are attempting to check
\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\displaystyle u,v$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\textstyle u,v$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\scriptstyle u,v$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle u,v$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}\in{x(i)}
for some
variable
i:\mathbb{I}
. The equational rules of XTT do not suggest any reductions for

x(i)
, so we might naïvely return a type error:
\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\displaystyle u,v$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\textstyle u,v$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\scriptstyle u,v$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle u,v$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}
can only be
an element of a product type, but
\mathsf{el}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle x(i)$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle x(i)$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle x(i)$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle x(i)$}\mathclose{}{)}}
appears to be neutral.

However, such a strategy is not complete in the presence of the boundary
separation rule. Suppose that in addition, we have
proofs
p:\mathsf{path}_{\_.\mathsf{set}}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle\hat{A},\hat{C}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle\hat{A},\hat{C}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\hat{A},\hat{C}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\hat{A},\hat{C}$}\mathclose{}{)}}
and
q:\mathsf{path}_{\_.\mathsf{set}}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle\hat{B},\hat{D}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle\hat{B},\hat{D}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\hat{B},\hat{D}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\hat{B},\hat{D}$}\mathclose{}{)}}
in scope. Then we may form the path

\lambda j.p(j)\mathbin{\hat{\times}}q(j):\mathsf{path}_{\_.\mathsf{set}}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle\hat{A}\mathbin{\hat{\times}}\hat{B},\hat{C}\mathbin{\hat{\times}}\hat{D}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle\hat{A}\mathbin{\hat{\times}}\hat{B},\hat{C}\mathbin{\hat{\times}}\hat{D}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\hat{A}\mathbin{\hat{\times}}\hat{B},\hat{C}\mathbin{\hat{\times}}\hat{D}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\hat{A}\mathbin{\hat{\times}}\hat{B},\hat{C}\mathbin{\hat{\times}}\hat{D}$}\mathclose{}{)}}
;
by boundary separation,
\mathsf{el}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle x(i)$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle x(i)$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle x(i)$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle x(i)$}\mathclose{}{)}}=\mathsf{el}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle p(i)$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle p(i)$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle p(i)$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle p(i)$}\mathclose{}{)}}\times\mathsf{el}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle q(i)$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle q(i)$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle q(i)$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle q(i)$}\mathclose{}{)}}

definitionally, and therefore we
must
proceed to check
u\in p(i)
and

v\in q(i)
(and possibly succeed).

Of course, an algorithm cannot guess out of thin air whether such
p,q
exist! A
way around this impasse, pioneered in
OTT
[
AM06
,
AMS07
]
, is to
ensure that from a path between
\hat{A}\mathbin{\hat{\times}}\hat{B}
and

\hat{C}\mathbin{\hat{\times}}\hat{D}
, we can
always
obtain a path between

\hat{A}
and
\hat{C}
. Under those circumstances, we have a uniform
strategy to type check terms on neutral equations between product types (
etc
.
):
ignore the proof of equality, and consider only its boundary.

This approach does
not
make sense for mathematical sets or spaces, since
there are more ways for two product sets to be equal than that their components
are equal, but it does make sense for closed universes, such as the
inductive-recursive universes of Martin-Löf
[
ML84
]
. We discuss
the semantic disadvantages of these closed universes in
Section
8.1
.

Concretely, we achieve this “injectivity up to paths” of type constructors in
XTT by including a “type-case” operator enabling intensional analysis of
sets
[
Con82
,
CZ84
,
HM95
]
.

2.4.
The LF signature of XTT

Thus far, we have presented the syntax of XTT as a series of informal inference
rules; formally, however, XTT is the bi-initial object in the 2-category of
models defined in Section
4
. As a middle ground
between those two styles, we now give a definition of XTT as a sequence of
constants (Figure
4
) in a logical framework (LF). By results
of Uemura
[
Uem19
,
Uem21
]
, these constants can be systematically elaborated
into the definitions of Section
4
, and
automatically induce a 2-category of models with a bi-initial object.
Conversely, connecting these LF constants to standard (but highly annotated)
inference rule presentations requires an
adequacy
theorem
[
HHP93
]
; we are using Uemura’s logical
framework
[
Uem19
,
Uem21
]
, which is adequate for a wide variety of type
theories.

2.4.1.
Uemura’s logical framework

Uemura’s LF is essentially a fragment of extensional dependent type theory; the
only important difference is that Uemura’s LF stratifies types into two kinds:
representable types
\star
and types
\Box
. Elements
\mathsf{J}:\star
correspond
to judgments that can be hypothesized (such as object-level term judgments),
whereas elements
\mathsf{J}:\Box
correspond to arbitrary judgments (such as
object-level type judgments, which generally cannot be hypothesized). We
summarize the rules of Uemura’s LF in Figure
3
, omitting the standard
definitional equalities for dependent products and extensional equality; readers
can consult Section 5 of
[
Uem19
]
for a thorough introduction.
7
7

7

Note that
[
Uem19
]
does not explicitly include dependent
sums, but these are present in the semantics and do not impact any of the
results of that paper.

Figure 3
.
A summary of Uemura’s logical framework.

In addition to the model theory and initiality result mentioned above, another
major advantage of using a logical framework is
higher-order abstract
syntax
, in which variable binders are encoded using the LF’s

\lambda
-abstractions over representable types. As a result, unlike inference
rules, LF encodings need not explicitly represent the object-level contexts, and
in fact automatically ensure that all operations are stable under substitution.

\displaystyle\begin{aligned} \mathbb{I}&:\star\\
\mathbb{F},\mathsf{tp}&:\Box\\
\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\displaystyle-$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\textstyle-$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\scriptstyle-$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle-$}\mathclose{}{]}}&:\mathbb{F}\to\star\\

The signature of XTT in Uemura’s logical framework. For space
reasons, we omit the remainder of the rules pertaining to the universe of
Bishop sets.

2.4.2.
The signature of XTT

In Figure
4
, we present XTT as a signature, or sequence of
constants, in Uemura’s LF. In accordance with the judgments-as-types methodology
[
HHP93
]
, we render each judgment of XTT as a type
constant in its LF signature. We encode the judgment
\Gamma\vdash r:\mathbb{I}
as a nullary
representable type with two elements; it is representable because XTT allows
context extension by dimension variables
\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle\Gamma,i:\mathbb{I}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle\Gamma,i:\mathbb{I}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\Gamma,i:\mathbb{I}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\Gamma,i:\mathbb{I}$}\mathclose{}{)}}
.

\displaystyle\mathbb{I}:\star

\displaystyle 0:\mathbb{I}

\displaystyle 1:\mathbb{I}

We encode the face formula judgment
\Gamma\vdash\phi:\mathbb{F}
as a (non-representable) type
equipped with a representable decoding function
\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\displaystyle-$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\textstyle-$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\scriptstyle-$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle-$}\mathclose{}{]}}
; contexts cannot be
extended by face formula variables, but we can extend contexts by an assumption
that
\phi
holds,
\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle\Gamma,\phi$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle\Gamma,\phi$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\Gamma,\phi$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\Gamma,\phi$}\mathclose{}{)}}
.

\displaystyle\mathbb{F}:\Box

\displaystyle\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\displaystyle-$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\textstyle-$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\scriptstyle-$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle-$}\mathclose{}{]}}:\mathbb{F}\to\star

Note that
\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\displaystyle-$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\textstyle-$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\scriptstyle-$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle-$}\mathclose{}{]}}
is silent in our earlier notation; in both the inference
rules and in Figure
4
, we suppress the instantiation of
partial elements by (the unique) proofs of
\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\displaystyle\phi$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\textstyle\phi$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\phi$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\phi$}\mathclose{}{]}}
.

Likewise, we encode
\Gamma\vdash A\ \mathit{type}
as a (non-representable) type and
\Gamma\vdash a:A
as a
representable type family.

\displaystyle\mathsf{tp}:\Box

\displaystyle\mathsf{tm}:\mathsf{tp}\to\star

We do not add constants for the equality judgments of XTT, as these are encoded
by LF equality at the corresponding type.

Finally, we encode the connectives and rules of XTT as constants, taking
advantage of the LF’s type structure for brevity. For example, the formation
rule for dependent products corresponds to the following LF constant:

A:\mathsf{tp},B:{\textstyle\prod}_{x:\mathsf{tm}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle A$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle A$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle A$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle A$}\mathclose{}{)}}}\mathsf{tp}\vdash\mathsf{pi}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle A,B$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle A,B$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle A,B$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle A,B$}\mathclose{}{)}}:\mathsf{tp}

The force of the remaining rules for dependent product types is simply to assert
an isomorphism between
\mathsf{tm}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mathsf{pi}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle A,B$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle A,B$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle A,B$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle A,B$}\mathclose{}{)}}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle\mathsf{pi}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle A,B$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle A,B$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle A,B$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle A,B$}\mathclose{}{)}}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mathsf{pi}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle A,B$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle A,B$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle A,B$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle A,B$}\mathclose{}{)}}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{pi}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle A,B$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle A,B$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle A,B$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle A,B$}\mathclose{}{)}}$}\mathclose{}{)}}
and

{\textstyle\prod}_{x:\mathsf{tm}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle A$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle A$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle A$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle A$}\mathclose{}{)}}}\mathsf{tm}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle B(a)$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle B(a)$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle B(a)$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle B(a)$}\mathclose{}{)}}
. To express this pattern concisely, we
introduce the notation
\Gamma\vdash f:A\cong B
for the following four constants:

\displaystyle\Gamma,x:A\vdash f^{\rightarrow}(x):B

\displaystyle\Gamma,x:B\vdash f^{\leftarrow}(x):A
\displaystyle\Gamma,x:A\vdash\_:f^{\leftarrow}(f^{\rightarrow}(x))=_{A}x

\displaystyle\Gamma,x:B\vdash\_:f^{\rightarrow}(f^{\leftarrow}(x))=_{B}x

Using this notation, we encode the introduction, elimination,
\beta
, and

\eta
laws of dependent products in one stroke:

A:\mathsf{tp},B:{\textstyle\prod}_{x:\mathsf{tm}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle A$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle A$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle A$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle A$}\mathclose{}{)}}}\mathsf{tp}\vdash\mathsf{pi/tm}:{\textstyle\prod}_{x:\mathsf{tm}{\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle A$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle A$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle A$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle A$}\mathclose{}{)}}}}\mathsf{tm}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle B(x)$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle B(x)$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle B(x)$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle B(x)$}\mathclose{}{)}}\cong\mathsf{tm}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mathsf{pi}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle A,B$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle A,B$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle A,B$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle A,B$}\mathclose{}{)}}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle\mathsf{pi}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle A,B$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle A,B$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle A,B$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle A,B$}\mathclose{}{)}}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mathsf{pi}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle A,B$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle A,B$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle A,B$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle A,B$}\mathclose{}{)}}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{pi}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle A,B$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle A,B$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle A,B$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle A,B$}\mathclose{}{)}}$}\mathclose{}{)}}

3.
Categorical preliminaries

All the categorical machinery we assume can be found in standard introductory
textbooks and
references
[
ML98
,
Bor94a
,
Bor94b
,
Bor10
,
Awo10
,
Joh02
]
;
in order to fix notations and render our presentation as self-contained as
possible, however, we have included a number of definitions. The beginning of
Section
3.1
recalls basic categorical definitions and
fixes notation, while Section
3.1.1
covers more specific facts
related to presheaves and representables.
The remaining sections discuss functorial semantics and the categorical
machinery necessary to account for the semantics of type theory.

We recommend only skimming this section on a first read, and return to it
as needed.

3.1.
Basic categorical definitions

{nota}

Given a category
\mathscr{C}
and objects
C,D:\mathscr{C}
, we write

\mathscr{C}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\displaystyle C,D$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\textstyle C,D$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\scriptstyle C,D$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle C,D$}\mathclose{}{]}}
for the collection of arrows between
C
and
D
. We will
also write
\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mathscr{C},\mathscr{D}$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\textstyle\mathscr{C},\mathscr{D}$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mathscr{C},\mathscr{D}$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathscr{C},\mathscr{D}$}\mathclose{}{]}}
for the
category
of functors

\mathscr{C}
\mathscr{D}
and natural transformations between them.
∎

{conv}

Conventionally, we write
\mathbf{Set}
and
\mathbf{Cat}
for the categories of sets and
categories respectively; of course, to be more precise, we should instead refer
to
\mathbf{Set}_{\alpha}
and
\mathbf{Cat}_{\alpha}
for some strongly inaccessible cardinal

\alpha
, or equivalently a Grothendieck universe
\mathscr{U}
. We leave the
resolution of these universes implicit, noting them explicitly in sensitive
places.

{nota}

We will write
\boldsymbol{\Delta}^{n}
for the
n
-simplex regarded as a category; in
particular,
\boldsymbol{\Delta}^{0}
is the terminal category

{defi}

[Cartesian arrow category]
We write
\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\Delta}^{1},\mathscr{C}$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\textstyle\boldsymbol{\Delta}^{1},\mathscr{C}$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{\Delta}^{1},\mathscr{C}$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{\Delta}^{1},\mathscr{C}$}\mathclose{}{]}}_{\mathit{cart}}
\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\Delta}^{1},\mathscr{C}$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\textstyle\boldsymbol{\Delta}^{1},\mathscr{C}$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{\Delta}^{1},\mathscr{C}$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{\Delta}^{1},\mathscr{C}$}\mathclose{}{]}}
for the wide
subcategory of arrows and
cartesian
squares between them.
Concretely, given
f,g:\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\Delta}^{1},\mathscr{C}$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\textstyle\boldsymbol{\Delta}^{1},\mathscr{C}$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{\Delta}^{1},\mathscr{C}$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{\Delta}^{1},\mathscr{C}$}\mathclose{}{]}}_{\mathit{cart}}
a morphism between them exhibits
f
as a
pullback of
g

{defi}

[Cartesian morphism]
Given a functor
\mathscr{E}
\mathscr{B}
p
, a morphism
E_{0}
E_{1}
f
is
cartesian
if for
every
E^{\prime}
E_{1}
g
and
pE^{\prime}
pE_{0}
u
such that
pg=pf\circ u
, there
exists a unique
E^{\prime}
E_{0}
h
over
u
such that
f\circ h=g
. Diagrammatically:

{defi}

[Opcartesian morphism]
Dually, given a functor
\mathscr{E}
\mathscr{B}
p
, a morphism

E_{0}
E_{1}
f
is
opcartesian
if for every
E_{0}
E^{\prime}
g
and

pE_{1}
pE^{\prime}
u
such that
pg=u\circ pf
, there
exists a unique factor
E_{1}
E^{\prime}
h
lying over
u
such that
h\circ f=g
:

{defi}

[Fibration]
A
fibration
is a functor
\mathscr{E}
\mathscr{B}
p
such that for each
morphism
B
pE
u
there exists a cartesian morphism

u^{*}E
E
u^{\dagger}{E}
lying over
u
:

u^{*}E
B
E
pE
u^{\dagger}{E}
u
\mathscr{E}
\mathscr{B}

We emphasize the property of an arrow being a fibration by using an open
triangular tip,
e.g
.

\mathscr{E}
\mathscr{B}
p
.
∎

{defi}

[Opfibration]
Dually, an
opfibration
is a functor
\mathscr{E}
\mathscr{B}
p
such that
for each morphism
pE
B
u
there exists an opcartesian morphism

E
u_{!}E
u^{\dagger}{E}
lying over
u
:

E
pE
u_{!}E
B
u^{\dagger}{E}
u
\mathscr{E}
\mathscr{B}

We emphasize the property of an arrow being an opfibration by using a filled triangular tip,
e.g
.

\mathscr{E}
\mathscr{B}
p
.
∎

Fact 4
.

The codomain functor

\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\Delta}^{1},\mathscr{C}$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\textstyle\boldsymbol{\Delta}^{1},\mathscr{C}$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{\Delta}^{1},\mathscr{C}$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{\Delta}^{1},\mathscr{C}$}\mathclose{}{]}}
\mathscr{C}
\partial_{1}
which sends
X
Y
f
to
Y

is always an opfibration, with opcartesian lifts implemented by postcomposition
(dependent sum).
∎

Fact 5
.

In a category
\mathscr{C}
with pullbacks, the codomain functor

\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\Delta}^{1},\mathscr{C}$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\textstyle\boldsymbol{\Delta}^{1},\mathscr{C}$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{\Delta}^{1},\mathscr{C}$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{\Delta}^{1},\mathscr{C}$}\mathclose{}{]}}
\mathscr{C}
\partial_{1}
is a fibration.
Cartesian lifts may are implemented by pullbacks in
\mathscr{C}
.
∎

The comma category
{F}\downarrow{G}
may be constructed more abstractly in terms
of the following (1-categorical) pullback in
\mathbf{Cat}
, the category of categories
and functors:

{F}\downarrow{G}
\mathscr{D}\times\mathscr{E}
\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\Delta}^{1},\mathscr{C}$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\textstyle\boldsymbol{\Delta}^{1},\mathscr{C}$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{\Delta}^{1},\mathscr{C}$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{\Delta}^{1},\mathscr{C}$}\mathclose{}{]}}
\mathscr{C}\times\mathscr{C}
\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle\partial_{0},\partial_{1}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle\partial_{0},\partial_{1}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\partial_{0},\partial_{1}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\partial_{0},\partial_{1}$}\mathclose{}{)}}
\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle F,G$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle F,G$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle F,G$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle F,G$}\mathclose{}{)}}

(0)

{nota}

Let
X:\mathscr{C}
; we will write
\boldsymbol{\Delta}^{0}
\mathscr{C}
\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\displaystyle X$}\mathclose{}{\}}}{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\textstyle X$}\mathclose{}{\}}}{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\scriptstyle X$}\mathclose{}{\}}}{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle X$}\mathclose{}{\}}}
for the constant functor
*\mapsto X
.
∎

{nota}

A common abuse of notation in the comma construction is that, when either
F

or
G
is the identity functor
\mathscr{C}
\mathscr{C}
\mathbf{id}_{\mathscr{C}}
, they
shall be written simply
\mathscr{C}
. For instance,
{\mathscr{C}}\downarrow{G}
is written for
{\mathbf{id}_{\mathscr{C}}}\downarrow{G}
.
∎

An important instance of the comma construction is the
slice
category.

{defi}

[Slice category]
Given an object
X:\mathscr{C}
, the
slice
or “over-category” of
\mathscr{C}

at
X
is the comma category
\mathscr{C}_{{/X}}={\mathscr{C}}\downarrow{\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\displaystyle X$}\mathclose{}{\}}}{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\textstyle X$}\mathclose{}{\}}}{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\scriptstyle X$}\mathclose{}{\}}}{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle X$}\mathclose{}{\}}}}
. The
objects of
\mathscr{C}_{{/X}}
can be seen to be arrows
Y
X
; morphisms
in the slice are commutative triangles.
∎

Fact 6
.

In a category with pullbacks
\mathscr{C}
, a morphism
X
Y
f
induces a functor

\mathscr{C}_{{/Y}}
\mathscr{C}_{{/X}}
f^{*}
sending
Z
Y
g
to

Z\times_{Y}X
X
f^{*}g
.
∎

{nota}

We will adopt a common abuse of notation and suppress the
weakening
functor

\mathscr{C}
\mathscr{C}_{{/X}}
!_{X}^{*}
when it is unambiguous.
∎

{defi}

Let
\kappa
be a regular cardinal; we say that a category
\mathscr{C}
is

\kappa
-(co)complete when
\mathscr{C}
has all (co)limits of
\kappa
-small diagrams;
a functor that preserves these (co)limits is called
\kappa
-(co)continuous.
When
\kappa
is omitted, a sufficiently large strongly inaccessible cardinal
is assumed.
∎

3.1.1.
Presheaves, representability, and discrete fibrations

{defi}

A
presheaf
on
\mathscr{C}
is a functor
\mathscr{C}^{\mathsf{op}}
\mathbf{Set}
F
; the
category of presheaves
\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mathscr{C}^{\mathsf{op}},\mathbf{Set}$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\textstyle\mathscr{C}^{\mathsf{op}},\mathbf{Set}$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mathscr{C}^{\mathsf{op}},\mathbf{Set}$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathscr{C}^{\mathsf{op}},\mathbf{Set}$}\mathclose{}{]}}
is written
\mathbf{Pr}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mathscr{C}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle\mathscr{C}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mathscr{C}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathscr{C}$}\mathclose{}{)}}
.
∎

Presheaves capture the geometric intuition of probing a space or other object
by small figures: the role of contexts and substitutions in (strict) type
theory supplies type theorists and logicians with a useful concrete intuition
for presheaves.
A more structural perspective on presheaves is, however, essential: the
category
\mathbf{Pr}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mathscr{C}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle\mathscr{C}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mathscr{C}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathscr{C}$}\mathclose{}{)}}
may be characterized universally as the

free cocompletion
of
\mathscr{C}
, equipping
\mathscr{C}
with new colimits.
When
\mathscr{C}
already has some colimits, it is important to note that the new
ones do
not
coincide with the old ones.

Construction 7

(The Yoneda embedding)
.

To be more precise, there is a universal functor

\mathscr{C}
\mathbf{Pr}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mathscr{C}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle\mathscr{C}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mathscr{C}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathscr{C}$}\mathclose{}{)}}
\mathsf{y}_{\mathscr{C}}
, called the
Yoneda embedding
,
taking each object
C:\mathscr{C}
to a “formal colimit”
\mathsf{y}_{\mathscr{C}}{C}=\mathscr{C}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\displaystyle\bullet,C$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\textstyle\bullet,C$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\bullet,C$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\bullet,C$}\mathclose{}{]}}

\mathscr{C}
\mathscr{E}
with

\mathsf{y}_{\mathscr{C}}
and a cocontinuous functor

an essentially unique way:

Lemma 8

(Yoneda)
.

For each presheaf
X:\mathbf{Pr}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mathscr{C}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle\mathscr{C}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mathscr{C}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathscr{C}$}\mathclose{}{)}}
, we have the following isomorphism:

\mathbf{Pr}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mathscr{C}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle\mathscr{C}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mathscr{C}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathscr{C}$}\mathclose{}{)}}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mathsf{y}_{\mathscr{C}}{C},X$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\textstyle\mathsf{y}_{\mathscr{C}}{C},X$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mathsf{y}_{\mathscr{C}}{C},X$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{y}_{\mathscr{C}}{C},X$}\mathclose{}{]}}\cong X\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle C$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle C$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle C$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle C$}\mathclose{}{)}}

As a consequence, the Yoneda embedding is full and faithful.

{defi}

A presheaf
X:\mathbf{Pr}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mathscr{C}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle\mathscr{C}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mathscr{C}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathscr{C}$}\mathclose{}{)}}
is called
representable
when it lies in
the essential image of
\mathsf{y}_{\mathscr{C}}
,
i.e
.

X
is isomorphic to
\mathsf{y}_{\mathscr{C}}{C}

for some
C:\mathscr{C}
.
∎

The notion of representable object is extended to maps in a canonical way, by
considering fibers over representable objects.

Representable natural transformations are a prime example of Grothendieck’s
“relative point of view”, extending a notion that is first defined on
objects to have sense on

It is useful to remark that the slice

.

Construction 9

(Category of elements)
.

The
category of elements

\mathscr{C}/X
of a presheaf
X:\mathbf{Pr}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mathscr{C}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle\mathscr{C}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mathscr{C}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathscr{C}$}\mathclose{}{)}}
has as

with

and morphisms
D/f^{*}x
C/x
f^{\dagger}x
for each
D
C
f
and

.
∎

In fact, the category of elements of a presheaf
X:\mathbf{Pr}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mathscr{C}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle\mathscr{C}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mathscr{C}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathscr{C}$}\mathclose{}{)}}
is the total
category of a
discrete fibration
over
\mathscr{C}
.

{defi}

A fibration
p:\mathscr{E}\to\mathscr{B}
is discrete if
pf=\mathbf{id}_{\mathscr{B}}

implies that
f=\mathbf{id}_{\mathscr{E}}
; equivalently, if the fibers of
p
are
discrete categories.
The collection of discrete fibrations over
\mathscr{C}
forms a full subcategory

\mathbf{DF}_{\mathscr{C}}\subseteq\mathbf{Fib}_{\mathscr{C}}\subseteq\mathbf{Cat}_{{/\mathscr{C}}}
, with
morphisms given by commuting triangles.
∎

Lemma 10
.

Let
X:\mathbf{Pr}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mathscr{C}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle\mathscr{C}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mathscr{C}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathscr{C}$}\mathclose{}{)}}
be a presheaf; the functor

\mathscr{C}/X
\mathscr{C}
p_{X}
that takes each

\mathscr{E}
\mathscr{C}
F
be a discrete fibration, we

in which each

is the pullback of

along
\boldsymbol{\Delta}^{0}
\mathscr{C}
!_{C}

As might be expected, the assignment

extends to a functor

\mathbf{Pr}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mathscr{C}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle\mathscr{C}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mathscr{C}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathscr{C}$}\mathclose{}{)}}

which is full, faithful, and
essentially surjective (
i.e
.
an equivalence of categories). Therefore

\mathbf{DF}_{\mathscr{C}}
may be used as an alternative to
\mathbf{Pr}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mathscr{C}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle\mathscr{C}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mathscr{C}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathscr{C}$}\mathclose{}{)}}
, and has its own

\mathscr{C}
\mathbf{DF}_{\mathscr{C}}
\mathsf{y}_{\mathscr{C}}
.

In the context of discrete fibrations, there is an alternative characterization
of representable maps in addition to
the Grothendieck-style extension of the essential image of the Yoneda embedding

\mathscr{C}
\mathbf{DF}_{\mathscr{C}}
\mathsf{y}_{\mathscr{C}}
to maps via pullbacks.

{}{}{}}}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\hss}\lxSVG@discardpath\lxSVG@closescope \hss}}\lxSVG@closescope\endpgfpicture}}:\mathbf{Cat}
has a
(non-fibered) right adjoint, which we may write
\partial_{0}f\dashv\mathbf{q}_{f}
.

In contrast with presheaves, it is natural to simultaneously work with discrete
fibrations over different base categories: we may write

\mathbf{DF}\subseteq\mathbf{Fib}\subseteq\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\Delta}^{1},\mathbf{Cat}$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\textstyle\boldsymbol{\Delta}^{1},\mathbf{Cat}$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{\Delta}^{1},\mathbf{Cat}$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{\Delta}^{1},\mathbf{Cat}$}\mathclose{}{]}}
for the category of fibrations
over arbitrary base, rendered a full subcategory of the category of arrows of

\mathbf{Cat}
. Therefore, a morphism of discrete fibrations is a commuting square:

\mathscr{E}_{0}
\mathscr{B}_{0}
p_{0}
\mathscr{E}_{1}
\mathscr{B}_{1}
\alpha_{1}
p_{1}
\alpha_{0}

Lemma 12
.

The map sending a discrete fibration to its base category
\mathbf{DF}
\mathbf{Cat}
\partial_{1}
is a
fibration. We will write
\mathbf{DF}_{\mathscr{C}}
for the fiber
\partial_{1}[\mathscr{C}]
.

3.1.3.
Philo-logie and Diaconescu’s theorem

Categories of presheaves
\mathscr{E}=\mathbf{Pr}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mathscr{C}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle\mathscr{C}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mathscr{C}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathscr{C}$}\mathclose{}{)}}
are complete, cocomplete,
locally cartesian closed, and exhibit certain non-trivial compatibilities
between certain limits and colimits which may be boiled down to the
existence of a classifying family for subobjects (monomorphisms). This

subobject classifier
is a monomorphism

\mathbf{1}_{\mathscr{E}}
\boldsymbol{\Omega}_{\mathscr{E}}
\mathsf{tr}_{\mathscr{E}}
that is universal
in the sense that all monomorphisms arise
in a unique way
from

\mathsf{tr}_{\mathscr{E}}
by pullback:

Y
X
m
\mathbf{1}_{\mathscr{E}}
\boldsymbol{\Omega}_{\mathscr{E}}
\mathsf{tr}_{\mathscr{E}}
{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}\exists!}\widetilde{m}

(0)

A category with these properties may be referred to as a
logos

following the terminology of Anel and Joyal
[
AJ21
]
, though we
defer the actual definition of logoi until Definition
3.1.3
. Recalling our
characterization of
\mathbf{Pr}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mathscr{C}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle\mathscr{C}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mathscr{C}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathscr{C}$}\mathclose{}{)}}
as the
free
cocompletion of
\mathscr{C}
,
we argue that the correct way to understand categories of presheaves is as a
class of logoi that are generated in a specific way: namely, all colimits are
added freely without imposing any relations.

We may also generate logoi in which the added colimits satisfy some relations;
historically, the most common way to do so is to augment the category
\mathscr{C}

with the data of a
coverage
. The canonical motivating example arises
when considering presheaves on the frame of open sets
\mathscr{O}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle X$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle X$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle X$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle X$}\mathclose{}{)}}
of a
topological space
X
. The logos of presheaves

not
have the geometrically correct colimits corresponding to the gluing
together of components of an open cover

{defi}

[Logos]

category
\mathscr{C}
; a morphism

for the 2-category of logoi, with 2-cells given by natural

(Direct image)

A flat functor is a generalization of the notion of left exact functor which may be used in case the
domain category
\mathscr{C}
is not finitely complete: in other words, a flat functor

\mathscr{C}
\mathscr{E}
is one that preserves “even the finite limits that don’t exist”. While the
general definition is slightly complex (see
[

), for our

\mathscr{C}
is finitely complete and when a flat

Flat functors play an essential role in the general gluing theorem for models of Martin-Löf type
theory into logoi developed by Sterling and Angiuli
[

]
which we have
applied in this paper.

3.1.4.
Topos–logos duality

Following the philosophy of Anel and Joyal
[
AJ21
]
, we have
(perhaps surprisingly to some readers) not referred to categories of presheaves
as “topoi”. This is because we prefer to think of a topos as a

geometrical
object, whereas a logos is
algebraic
in nature: for
instance, Diaconescu’s Theorem (Theorem
15
) shows that the
category of presheaves is an invariant form of the
theory
of flat
functors in the style of Lawvere’s functorial semantics
[
Law63
]
.

It is instructive to start from the prototype of geometry–algebra duality embodied in the relationship between (sober) topological spaces and their
frames of open sets; in this case, the frame of opens is an algebraic object,
and the corresponding space is its geometric dual. By an analogy that may
be substantiated in a precise way, a logos is the algebraic object
corresponding to a topos, which is in contrast a kind of generalized space.

The duality between topoi and logoi is captured in a formal equivalence of
categories

, taking a topos to its

object of study
[

,

: sheaves should be thought of as
algebraic data varying over a (generalized) space, including both topological

and

recalling that any sober space corresponds to an essentially unique

enveloping topos

[

]
.

On the other hand, the algebraic perspective of
logoi
and their
algebraic morphisms is the most germane to this paper, so we do not refer to
topoi in subsequent sections.

3.2.
Functorial semantics of dependent type theory à la Uemura

Classically, the notion of an “algebraic theory” was understood in terms of
sets of operations and equations. For instance, the theory of monoids may be
written in terms of two operations:
\varepsilon
of arity
[0]
and
\odot
of
arity
[2]
. Then, a set of equations is imposed on the set of trees generated
by
\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\varepsilon,\odot$}\mathclose{}{\}}}{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\textstyle\varepsilon,\odot$}\mathclose{}{\}}}{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\varepsilon,\odot$}\mathclose{}{\}}}{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\varepsilon,\odot$}\mathclose{}{\}}}
to express the associativity and unit laws of a
monoid.
A model of a theory in this old-fashioned sense was then a
structure
comprising the following data:

(1)

a carrier set
A
,

(2)

a map
\varepsilon_{A}:1\to A
,

(3)

a map
\odot_{A}:A\times A\to A
,

(4)

subject to the following equations:

\displaystyle\odot_{A}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle\varepsilon_{A},x$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle\varepsilon_{A},x$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\varepsilon_{A},x$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\varepsilon_{A},x$}\mathclose{}{)}}

\displaystyle=x

\displaystyle\odot_{A}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle x,\varepsilon_{A}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle x,\varepsilon_{A}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle x,\varepsilon_{A}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle x,\varepsilon_{A}$}\mathclose{}{)}}

\displaystyle=x

\displaystyle\odot_{A}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle\odot_{A}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle x,y$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle x,y$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle x,y$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle x,y$}\mathclose{}{)}},z$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle\odot_{A}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle x,y$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle x,y$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle x,y$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle x,y$}\mathclose{}{)}},z$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\odot_{A}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle x,y$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle x,y$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle x,y$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle x,y$}\mathclose{}{)}},z$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\odot_{A}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle x,y$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle x,y$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle x,y$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle x,y$}\mathclose{}{)}},z$}\mathclose{}{)}}

\displaystyle=\odot_{A}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle x,\odot_{A}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle y,z$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle y,z$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle y,z$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle y,z$}\mathclose{}{)}}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle x,\odot_{A}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle y,z$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle y,z$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle y,z$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle y,z$}\mathclose{}{)}}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle x,\odot_{A}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle y,z$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle y,z$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle y,z$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle y,z$}\mathclose{}{)}}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle x,\odot_{A}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle y,z$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle y,z$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle y,z$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle y,z$}\mathclose{}{)}}$}\mathclose{}{)}}

Models in this sense arrange themselves into a category, with morphisms given
by functions between carrier sets that commute with the specified maps; of
course, this is nothing more than the category of monoids in
\mathbf{Set}
. Generally,
one considers models in categories other than
\mathbf{Set}
, a notion that makes
sense for any category
\mathscr{C}
having the requisite structure (in this case,
finite products).

However, there are many other collections of operations and axioms that
equally well express the concept of
monoid
, evidently exhibiting the
same categories of models. For instance, one may use the set of operations

\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mathrm{list}_{n}\mid n\in\mathbb{N}$}\mathclose{}{\}}}{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\textstyle\mathrm{list}_{n}\mid n\in\mathbb{N}$}\mathclose{}{\}}}{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mathrm{list}_{n}\mid n\in\mathbb{N}$}\mathclose{}{\}}}{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{list}_{n}\mid n\in\mathbb{N}$}\mathclose{}{\}}}\cup\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\odot$}\mathclose{}{\}}}{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\textstyle\odot$}\mathclose{}{\}}}{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\odot$}\mathclose{}{\}}}{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\odot$}\mathclose{}{\}}}
where each
operation
\mathrm{list}_{n}
has arity
[n]
. Lawvere famously observed that
none of the important computations in universal algebra actually depend on
which specific operations and axioms are used to encode a theory, advocating a
perspective that regards the presentations above
not
as the theories
themselves, but as structures lying over the theories.

A
theory
for Lawvere is a category
\mathbb{T}
closed under certain structures
(
e.g
.
finite products, finite limits,
etc
.
); a model of a theory in a category

\mathscr{C}
is a functor
\mathbb{T}
\mathscr{C}
preserving (finite products,
finite limits,
etc
.
). A collection of operations and axioms that generates a
theory is called a
equational presentation
of that theory.

Lawvere’s functorial perspective on theories and their models is called the

functorial semantics

[
Law63
]
.
Lawvere has observed that many of the fundamental operations by which new
theories are constructed from old theories are unnatural to describe in terms of
presentations, but are simple at the level of categories and functors.
One may continue to
present
theories
\mathbb{T}
by sets of operations and
axioms as before, but the spirit of the functorial method is to freely adopt
whichever presentation is most useful in a specific context.

3.2.1.
Natural models, the judgmental essence of strict type theory

We recall from Definition
3.1.1
the notion of a

representable natural transformation
of presheaves: it is a family of
presheaves that, at every fiber over a representable object, is a
representable object. This notion, which first arose in the context of algebraic
geometry in the Grothendieck school
[
AGV72
]
, plays a fundamental role in
the semantics of dependent type theory as well as the categorical study of set
theory and
universes
[
Awo18b
,
Awo08
,
Str05
,
Str14b
]
.

From the type theoretic perspective, the importance of representable maps is
easy to explain. In type theory, the basic objects under consideration are
contexts
\Gamma
, types in context
\Gamma\vdash A
, and typed terms in
context
\Gamma\vdash a:A
. The collection of types carries an action for
each substitution
\Delta
\Gamma
\gamma
of contexts, and so does the
collection of elements: we have
\Delta\vdash\gamma^{*}A
and
\Delta\vdash\gamma^{*}a:\gamma^{*}A
. Moreover, while there is no context that represents the
collection of all types, for any specific type
\Gamma\vdash A
, we have a context

\Gamma.A
that represents the
elements
of the type
A
.

This type theoretic situation can be captured mathematically in three steps:

(1)

First of all, the collection of contexts may be organized into a
category
\mathscr{C}
with morphisms given by simultaneous substitutions.

(2)

Next, the collection of types may be viewed as a presheaf

\mathbf{T}_{\mathscr{C}}:\mathbf{Pr}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mathscr{C}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle\mathscr{C}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mathscr{C}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathscr{C}$}\mathclose{}{)}}
: a section
A\in\mathbf{T}_{\mathscr{C}}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle\Gamma$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle\Gamma$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\Gamma$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\Gamma$}\mathclose{}{)}}
is exactly a type
\Gamma\vdash A
, and the
functorial action implements substitution on types. Likewise, the
collection of typed elements is a presheaf indexed in the presheaf of
types,
i.e
.
a family

\widetilde{\mathbf{T}}_{\mathscr{C}}
\mathbf{T}_{\mathscr{C}}
\boldsymbol{\uptau}_{\mathscr{C}}
.

(3)

From the perspective of the Yoneda lemma, one may think of contexts as
representable presheaves
\Gamma:\mathbf{Pr}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mathscr{C}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle\mathscr{C}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mathscr{C}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathscr{C}$}\mathclose{}{)}}
, and a type in context

\Gamma
is a morphism
\Gamma
\mathbf{T}_{\mathscr{C}}
A
. We therefore
obtain representing contexts
\Gamma.A
for each such type
A
by requiring
that the family

\widetilde{\mathbf{T}}_{\mathscr{C}}
\mathbf{T}_{\mathscr{C}}
\boldsymbol{\uptau}_{\mathscr{C}}
be a
representable natural transformation:

\Gamma.A
\Gamma
p_{A}
\widetilde{\mathbf{T}}_{\mathscr{C}}
\mathbf{T}_{\mathscr{C}}
q_{A}
\boldsymbol{\uptau}_{\mathscr{C}}
A

(0)

The map
\Gamma.A
\Gamma
p_{A}
is the
weakening
substitution, and
the map
\Gamma.A
\widetilde{\mathbf{T}}_{\mathscr{C}}
q_{A}
is the
variable
term. By
chasing Diagram
0
, it is easy to see that the type of the term

q_{A}
is
p_{A}^{*}A
as expected.
The structure defined above captures the decisive judgmental aspects of
dependent type theory, and has been referred to by Awodey as a
natural
model
: natural in both the informal sense, and in the sense that it is defined
in terms of a representable
natural
transformation.

{defiC}

[
[
Awo18b
]
]
A natural model is a category
\mathscr{C}
with a terminal object, together with a representable natural transformation in
\mathbf{Pr}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mathscr{C}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle\mathscr{C}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mathscr{C}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathscr{C}$}\mathclose{}{)}}
.
∎

3.2.2.
Representable map categories and the semantics of type theory

A given type theory is more than just a natural model in the sense of
Definition
3.2.1
: one must also specify other generators,
such as type connectives and their elements. Most type connectives can be
specified by writing down a family in
\mathbf{Pr}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mathscr{C}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle\mathscr{C}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mathscr{C}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathscr{C}$}\mathclose{}{)}}
and then asking for a
cartesian square between that family and the natural model. This raises some questions:

(1)

What kinds of structures can be added to the notion of a natural model
and still give rise to a type theory?

(2)

What is a morphism between models of such a type theory?

Uemura proposes to answer this question by developing a notion of “general
type theory” and associated functorial semantics
[
Uem19
,
Uem21
]
; while
Lawvere defines an algebraic theory to be (roughly) a category with finite
products, Uemura defines a
type
theory
\mathbb{T}
to be a

representable map category
, which is a lex category
\mathscr{C}
together
with a distinguished class
\mathcal{R}
of “representable maps” which
captures the decisive aspects of the class of representable natural
transformations in presheaf logoi.

{defi}

A class of representable maps in a lex category
\mathscr{C}
is a collection of maps

\mathcal{R}
with the following closure conditions:

(1)

Each identity map is representable, and the composition of representable maps is representable.

(2)

Every pullback of a representable map along an arbitrary map is representable.

(3)

Pullback along a representable map has a right adjoint, pushforward.
∎

{nota}

In particular, if the terminal map
X
\mathbf{1}_{\mathscr{C}}
is
representable, then all exponentials (internal homs) out of
X
may be
computed by pushforward, which we may write either
X\Rightarrow Y
or
\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{\llbracket}\hbox{$\displaystyle X,Y$}\mathclose{}{\rrbracket}}{\mathopen{}{\llbracket}\hbox{$\textstyle X,Y$}\mathclose{}{\rrbracket}}{\mathopen{}{\llbracket}\hbox{$\scriptstyle X,Y$}\mathclose{}{\rrbracket}}{\mathopen{}{\llbracket}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle X,Y$}\mathclose{}{\rrbracket}}
.
∎

{defi}

A representable map category is a lex category
\mathscr{C}
together with a class

\mathcal{R}
of representable maps in
\mathscr{C}
; a
representable map
functor
between two representable map categories is a functor between the
underlying categories that takes representable maps to representable maps.
∎

Remark 16
.

Every lex category
\mathscr{C}
can be thought of as a very weak kind of extensional type theory, in which dependent types are maps and substitutions are given by pullback. A representable map structure on
\mathscr{C}
does nothing more than enrich this language as follows:

(1)

There is a class of
small
types called “representable” types.

(2)

Representable types are closed under dependent sums.

(3)

Types are closed under dependent products with representable base.

The “type theory” of a representable map category
\mathbb{T}=\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mathscr{C},\mathcal{R}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle\mathscr{C},\mathcal{R}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mathscr{C},\mathcal{R}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathscr{C},\mathcal{R}$}\mathclose{}{)}}
can be thought of as a logical framework in the
sense of
[
HHP93
,
NPS90
]
, in
which hypothetical judgments are represented by pushforward.
From this
perspective, it is most appropriate to refer to arbitrary objects and
families in
\mathbb{T}
as judgments, following the “judgments as types”
philosophy of Harper, Honsell, and
Plotkin
[
HHP93
]
.

∎

{exa}

[The walking natural model]
The type theory with judgments for types and terms is specified by the
representable map category
\mathbb{T}
generated by a single representable map

\widetilde{\mathbf{T}}
\mathbf{T}
\boldsymbol{\uptau}
.
∎

{exa}

\mathbf{Pr}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mathscr{C}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle\mathscr{C}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mathscr{C}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathscr{C}$}\mathclose{}{)}}
supports the structure of a representable map category with the class of
representable maps given by representable natural transformations.
∎

The classic notion of a representable map in a category of presheaves is of
course an instance, giving rise to the “canonical representable structures”
on
\mathbf{Pr}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mathscr{C}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle\mathscr{C}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mathscr{C}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathscr{C}$}\mathclose{}{)}}
and
\mathbf{DF}_{\mathscr{C}}
.

{exa}

\mathbf{DF}_{\mathscr{C}}
supports the structure of a representable map category, with
representable maps given by a functors between discrete fibrations that have
a non-fibered right
adjoint
[

ABSS14

In addition to these requirements, a morphism of models should also preserve
