{defi}

[Morphism of Models]
A morphism between
\mathbb{T}
\mathbf{DF}_{\mathscr{C}}
\mathscr{M}_{\mathscr{C}}
and

\mathbb{T}
\mathbf{DF}_{\mathscr{D}}
\mathscr{M}_{\mathscr{D}}
is a functor
\mathscr{C}
\mathscr{D}
F

preserving the terminal object, together with an assignment of functors

X_{\mathscr{C}}
X_{\mathscr{D}}
X_{F}
lying over
F
, natural in

X:\mathbb{T}
, such that each representable map
X
Y
f
satisfies the
Beck-Chevalley condition.
∎

{nota}

Let
\mathscr{M}_{\mathscr{C}}
\mathscr{M}_{\mathscr{D}}
\mathscr{M}_{F}
be a morphism of

\mathbb{T}
-models; given
X:\mathbb{T},x:X_{\mathscr{C}}
, we will abusively write

F{x}
for
X_{F}{x}
.
∎

Because morphisms of models necessarily require preservation of context
extensions only up to isomorphism, a higher level of morphism naturally arises,
lending the collection of models
\mathbf{Mod}_{\mathbb{T}}
with the structure of a
2-category.

{defi}

[2-morphisms of models]
Given a pair of morphisms
\mathscr{M}_{\mathscr{C}}
\mathscr{M}_{\mathscr{D}}
\mathscr{M}_{F},\mathscr{M}_{G}
, a 2-morphism

\mathscr{M}_{F}
\mathscr{M}_{G}
\mathscr{M}_{\alpha}
is a natural transformation
F
G
\alpha
between the underlying functors such
that for each
X:\mathbb{T}
, there exists a
necessarily unique
natural transformation

X_{F}
X_{G}
X_{\alpha}
lying over
\alpha
.
∎

Remark 17
.

The uniqueness of the map
X_{F}
X_{G}
X_{\alpha}

lying over
\alpha
is ensured by the discreteness of
X_{\mathscr{D}}
.
Summarizing, the existence of
X_{\alpha}
is nothing more than the

condition
that for each
x:X_{\mathscr{C}}
lying over
\Gamma:\mathscr{C}
, the following equation obtains:

\alpha_{\Gamma}^{*}{Gx}=F{x}\qed

Theorem 18
.

The 2-category of models
\mathbf{Mod}_{\mathbb{T}}
has a
bi-initial
object: an object
I
such that
for each
X:\mathbf{Mod}_{\mathbb{T}}
, the category of morphisms
\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\displaystyle I,X$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\textstyle I,X$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\scriptstyle I,X$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle I,X$}\mathclose{}{]}}
is contractible.

This bi-initial object is the
democratic heart
of the embedding

\mathbb{T}
\mathbf{DF}_{\mathbb{T}}
\mathsf{y}
: the smallest full subcategory of
\mathbb{T}

containing the terminal object and closed under context extension.
The universal property of this bi-initial object ensures that there is at most one
morphism
\mathscr{M}_{\mathscr{I}}
\mathscr{M}_{\mathscr{C}}
for
each
\mathscr{M}_{\mathscr{C}}
, up to a unique invertible 2-morphism.

3.3.
Left lifting structures, orthogonality, and separation

\mathscr{E}
be a category with finite limits. We call
an object

\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{\llbracket}\hbox{$\displaystyle X,Y$}\mathclose{}{\rrbracket}}{\mathopen{}{\llbracket}\hbox{$\textstyle X,Y$}\mathclose{}{\rrbracket}}{\mathopen{}{\llbracket}\hbox{$\scriptstyle X,Y$}\mathclose{}{\rrbracket}}{\mathopen{}{\llbracket}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle X,Y$}\mathclose{}{\rrbracket}}

from

ABFJ18

{defi}

[Internal pullback hom]
Let
A
B
f
and
X
Y
g
be morphisms in
\mathscr{E}
such that

A,B
are both exponentiable. Then, the
internal pullback hom
of
f

and
g
is the cartesian gap map
\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{\llbracket}\hbox{$\displaystyle B,X$}\mathclose{}{\rrbracket}}{\mathopen{}{\llbracket}\hbox{$\textstyle B,X$}\mathclose{}{\rrbracket}}{\mathopen{}{\llbracket}\hbox{$\scriptstyle B,X$}\mathclose{}{\rrbracket}}{\mathopen{}{\llbracket}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle B,X$}\mathclose{}{\rrbracket}}
\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{\llbracket}\hbox{$\displaystyle A,X$}\mathclose{}{\rrbracket}}{\mathopen{}{\llbracket}\hbox{$\textstyle A,X$}\mathclose{}{\rrbracket}}{\mathopen{}{\llbracket}\hbox{$\scriptstyle A,X$}\mathclose{}{\rrbracket}}{\mathopen{}{\llbracket}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle A,X$}\mathclose{}{\rrbracket}}\times_{\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{\llbracket}\hbox{$\displaystyle A,Y$}\mathclose{}{\rrbracket}}{\mathopen{}{\llbracket}\hbox{$\textstyle A,Y$}\mathclose{}{\rrbracket}}{\mathopen{}{\llbracket}\hbox{$\scriptstyle A,Y$}\mathclose{}{\rrbracket}}{\mathopen{}{\llbracket}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle A,Y$}\mathclose{}{\rrbracket}}}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{\llbracket}\hbox{$\displaystyle B,Y$}\mathclose{}{\rrbracket}}{\mathopen{}{\llbracket}\hbox{$\textstyle B,Y$}\mathclose{}{\rrbracket}}{\mathopen{}{\llbracket}\hbox{$\scriptstyle B,Y$}\mathclose{}{\rrbracket}}{\mathopen{}{\llbracket}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle B,Y$}\mathclose{}{\rrbracket}}
\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{\llangle}\hbox{$\displaystyle f,g$}\mathclose{}{\rrangle}}{\mathopen{}{\llangle}\hbox{$\textstyle f,g$}\mathclose{}{\rrangle}}{\mathopen{}{\llangle}\hbox{$\scriptstyle f,g$}\mathclose{}{\rrangle}}{\mathopen{}{\llangle}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle f,g$}\mathclose{}{\rrangle}}

{defi}

[Internal orthogonality]
A map
A
B
f
is
internally left orthogonal
to

X
Y
g
, written
f\mathrel{\mathrel{\reflectbox{\rotatebox[origin]{90.0}{$\Vdash$}}}}g
, if we have
\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle Z\times f$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle Z\times f$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle Z\times f$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle Z\times f$}\mathclose{}{)}}\mathrel{\bot}g
for every
Z:\mathscr{E}
.
∎

{lemC}

[
[

, Definition 3.2.5]
]

f

Y
g
with

exponentiable; then

f\mathrel{\mathrel{\reflectbox{\rotatebox[origin]{90.0}{$\Vdash$}}}}g
iff the internal pullback hom
\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{\llangle}\hbox{$\displaystyle f,g$}\mathclose{}{\rrangle}}{\mathopen{}{\llangle}\hbox{$\textstyle f,g$}\mathclose{}{\rrangle}}{\mathopen{}{\llangle}\hbox{$\scriptstyle f,g$}\mathclose{}{\rrangle}}{\mathopen{}{\llangle}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle f,g$}\mathclose{}{\rrangle}}
is an isomorphism.
∎

{exa}

[Intensional identity types]
In order to formulate the elimination of intensional identity types in a natural model,
Awodey
[
Awo18a
]
uses a left lifting structure. More generally,
most “pattern-matching” style elimination rules in type theory can be formulated as a left
lifting structure
[
GKNB20
]
.

Remark 19
.

A left lifting structure
j:f\pitchfork g
exhibits
f
as internally left orthogonal to
g
when
j
is simultaneously a retraction.
∎

Because both left lifting structures and orthogonality conditions may be
expressed in the language of finite limits as above, it is justified to freely
extend a representable map category
\mathbb{T}
by either
f\mathrel{\mathrel{\reflectbox{\rotatebox[origin]{90.0}{$\Vdash$}}}}g
or
j:f\pitchfork g
.
In many cases, however, an orthogonality condition or lifting structure will
need to be expressed in the free cocompletion
\mathbf{Pr}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mathbb{T}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle\mathbb{T}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mathbb{T}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathbb{T}$}\mathclose{}{)}}
because it may
involve colimits that don’t exist in
\mathbb{T}
; when defining a representable
map category by a sequence of clauses, it is not
a priori
clear that
this move is legitimate.

We will therefore characterize a useful class of orthogonality and lifting
conditions on
\mathbf{Pr}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mathscr{C}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle\mathscr{C}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mathscr{C}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathscr{C}$}\mathclose{}{)}}
which may be unravelled into a suitable condition
on a lex category
\mathscr{C}
, expressible using the language of finite limits.

Lemma 20
.

Let
\mathscr{I}
be a small category such that limits of
\mathscr{I}
-diagrams exist in
\mathscr{C}
;
let
\mathscr{I}
\mathscr{C}
\Phi_{\bullet}
be a diagram such that for
each
i:\mathscr{I}
, the object
\Phi_{i}
is exponentiable. We will write

\hat{\Phi}_{\infty}
for the colimit of
\Phi_{\bullet}
taken in
\mathbf{Pr}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mathscr{C}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle\mathscr{C}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mathscr{C}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathscr{C}$}\mathclose{}{)}}
,

i.e
.

\hat{\Phi}_{\infty}=\operatorname{colim}_{\mathscr{I}}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mathsf{y}_{\mathscr{C}}{\Phi_{\bullet}}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle\mathsf{y}_{\mathscr{C}}{\Phi_{\bullet}}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mathsf{y}_{\mathscr{C}}{\Phi_{\bullet}}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{y}_{\mathscr{C}}{\Phi_{\bullet}}$}\mathclose{}{)}}
. Now let

\hbox to36.93pt{\vbox to12.16pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 7.0139pt\lower-1.94443pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} {}{}{}{}{{{}}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\hbox{\hbox{{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} {{}{}{{

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces
}{{{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@transformcm{1.0}{0.0}{0.0}{1.0}{-7.0139pt}{0.0pt}\lxSVG@begingroup@{transform} \pgfsys@hbox{60}\lxSVG@closescope }}}

3.4.
Using Artin gluing to prove canonicity

In this section, we give a gentle introduction to the use of Artin gluing for
proving ordinary canonicity results in order to set the stage for our more
sophisticated application. Let
\mathscr{C}
be the free cartesian closed category
generated by a base type
\mathsf{ans}:\mathscr{C}
and two constants

\mathbf{1}_{\mathscr{C}}
\mathsf{ans}
\mathsf{yes},\mathsf{no}
. We wish to prove the
following
closed canonicity
theorem:

Proposition 21

(Closed canonicity)
.

Let
\mathbf{1}_{\mathscr{C}}
\mathsf{ans}
a
be a morphism in
\mathscr{C}
; then
either
a=\mathsf{yes}
or
a=\mathsf{no}
.

This can be proved by means of
logical predicates
/ the
Tait’s method of
computability

[
Tai67
]
. Peter Freyd observed that the structural aspects of Tait’s method
can be captured by the well-known categorical construct of Artin gluing.
We define a new category
\mathscr{P}
that will serve as a domain of
interpretation for a logical predicates model of
\mathscr{C}
. An object of

\mathscr{P}
is defined to be a pair
\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle C,\tilde{C}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle C,\tilde{C}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle C,\tilde{C}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle C,\tilde{C}$}\mathclose{}{)}}
with
C:\mathscr{C}
and

\tilde{C}\subseteq\mathscr{C}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mathbf{1}_{\mathscr{C}},C$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\textstyle\mathbf{1}_{\mathscr{C}},C$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mathbf{1}_{\mathscr{C}},C$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathbf{1}_{\mathscr{C}},C$}\mathclose{}{]}}
, and a morphism

\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle C,\tilde{C}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle C,\tilde{C}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle C,\tilde{C}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle C,\tilde{C}$}\mathclose{}{)}}
\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle D,\tilde{D}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle D,\tilde{D}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle D,\tilde{D}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle D,\tilde{D}$}\mathclose{}{)}}
is given by a morphism

\hbox to20.42pt{\vbox to10.31pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 3.93124pt\lower-0.09998pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} {}{}{}{}{{{}}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\hbox{\hbox{{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} {{}{}{{

that preserves the predicates in the sense that the
following commutative diagram exists:

\tilde{C}
\mathscr{C}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mathbf{1}_{\mathscr{C}},C$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\textstyle\mathbf{1}_{\mathscr{C}},C$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mathbf{1}_{\mathscr{C}},C$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathbf{1}_{\mathscr{C}},C$}\mathclose{}{]}}
\subseteq
\tilde{D}
\mathscr{C}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mathbf{1}_{\mathscr{C}},D$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\textstyle\mathbf{1}_{\mathscr{C}},D$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mathbf{1}_{\mathscr{C}},D$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathbf{1}_{\mathscr{C}},D$}\mathclose{}{]}}
\subseteq
\mathscr{C}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mathbf{1}_{\mathscr{C}},f$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\textstyle\mathbf{1}_{\mathscr{C}},f$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mathbf{1}_{\mathscr{C}},f$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathbf{1}_{\mathscr{C}},f$}\mathclose{}{]}}

The diagram above states the traditional condition for extending a logical predicate
to open terms: for any closed
c\in\tilde{C}
, the evaluation
f(c)
is in

\tilde{D}
.

We have a
fibration

\mathscr{P}
\mathscr{C}
p
sending

\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle C,\tilde{C}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle C,\tilde{C}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle C,\tilde{C}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle C,\tilde{C}$}\mathclose{}{)}}
to
C
; moreover, we can show that
\mathscr{P}
is
cartesian closed and the fibration
p
preserves the cartesian closed
structure. The latter amounts to constructing products and exponentials in
\mathscr{P}

whose
\mathscr{C}
-parts are the corresponding products and exponentials from the
syntactic category, which is always built into logical predicates arguments.

In functorial semantics, a logical predicates model of
\mathscr{C}
is the same as
a functor
\mathscr{C}
\mathscr{P}
that preserves the cartesian closed
structure for which the composite with the fibration

\mathscr{P}
\mathscr{C}
p
is the identity,
i.e
.
a section of
p
. Because
\mathscr{C}
is the

free
cartesian closed category generated by

\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mathsf{ans},\mathsf{yes},\mathsf{no}$}\mathclose{}{\}}}{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\textstyle\mathsf{ans},\mathsf{yes},\mathsf{no}$}\mathclose{}{\}}}{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mathsf{ans},\mathsf{yes},\mathsf{no}$}\mathclose{}{\}}}{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{ans},\mathsf{yes},\mathsf{no}$}\mathclose{}{\}}}
, such a functor is
uniquely
determined by
a choice of an object
\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{\llbracket}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mathsf{ans}$}\mathclose{}{\rrbracket}}{\mathopen{}{\llbracket}\hbox{$\textstyle\mathsf{ans}$}\mathclose{}{\rrbracket}}{\mathopen{}{\llbracket}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mathsf{ans}$}\mathclose{}{\rrbracket}}{\mathopen{}{\llbracket}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{ans}$}\mathclose{}{\rrbracket}}:\mathscr{P}
such that

p\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{\llbracket}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mathsf{ans}$}\mathclose{}{\rrbracket}}{\mathopen{}{\llbracket}\hbox{$\textstyle\mathsf{ans}$}\mathclose{}{\rrbracket}}{\mathopen{}{\llbracket}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mathsf{ans}$}\mathclose{}{\rrbracket}}{\mathopen{}{\llbracket}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{ans}$}\mathclose{}{\rrbracket}}=\mathsf{ans}
, and a choice of constants

\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{\llbracket}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mathsf{yes}$}\mathclose{}{\rrbracket}}{\mathopen{}{\llbracket}\hbox{$\textstyle\mathsf{yes}$}\mathclose{}{\rrbracket}}{\mathopen{}{\llbracket}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mathsf{yes}$}\mathclose{}{\rrbracket}}{\mathopen{}{\llbracket}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{yes}$}\mathclose{}{\rrbracket}},\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{\llbracket}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mathsf{no}$}\mathclose{}{\rrbracket}}{\mathopen{}{\llbracket}\hbox{$\textstyle\mathsf{no}$}\mathclose{}{\rrbracket}}{\mathopen{}{\llbracket}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mathsf{no}$}\mathclose{}{\rrbracket}}{\mathopen{}{\llbracket}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{no}$}\mathclose{}{\rrbracket}}
configured as follows:

\mathbf{1}_{\mathscr{P}}
\mathbf{1}_{\mathscr{C}}
\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{\llbracket}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mathsf{ans}$}\mathclose{}{\rrbracket}}{\mathopen{}{\llbracket}\hbox{$\textstyle\mathsf{ans}$}\mathclose{}{\rrbracket}}{\mathopen{}{\llbracket}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mathsf{ans}$}\mathclose{}{\rrbracket}}{\mathopen{}{\llbracket}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{ans}$}\mathclose{}{\rrbracket}}
\mathsf{ans}
\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{\llbracket}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mathsf{yes}$}\mathclose{}{\rrbracket}}{\mathopen{}{\llbracket}\hbox{$\textstyle\mathsf{yes}$}\mathclose{}{\rrbracket}}{\mathopen{}{\llbracket}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mathsf{yes}$}\mathclose{}{\rrbracket}}{\mathopen{}{\llbracket}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{yes}$}\mathclose{}{\rrbracket}}
\mathsf{yes}
\mathbf{1}_{\mathscr{P}}
\mathbf{1}_{\mathscr{C}}
\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{\llbracket}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mathsf{ans}$}\mathclose{}{\rrbracket}}{\mathopen{}{\llbracket}\hbox{$\textstyle\mathsf{ans}$}\mathclose{}{\rrbracket}}{\mathopen{}{\llbracket}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mathsf{ans}$}\mathclose{}{\rrbracket}}{\mathopen{}{\llbracket}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{ans}$}\mathclose{}{\rrbracket}}
\mathsf{ans}
\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{\llbracket}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mathsf{no}$}\mathclose{}{\rrbracket}}{\mathopen{}{\llbracket}\hbox{$\textstyle\mathsf{no}$}\mathclose{}{\rrbracket}}{\mathopen{}{\llbracket}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mathsf{no}$}\mathclose{}{\rrbracket}}{\mathopen{}{\llbracket}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{no}$}\mathclose{}{\rrbracket}}
\mathsf{no}
\mathscr{P}
\mathscr{C}

We then choose
\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{\llbracket}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mathsf{ans}$}\mathclose{}{\rrbracket}}{\mathopen{}{\llbracket}\hbox{$\textstyle\mathsf{ans}$}\mathclose{}{\rrbracket}}{\mathopen{}{\llbracket}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mathsf{ans}$}\mathclose{}{\rrbracket}}{\mathopen{}{\llbracket}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{ans}$}\mathclose{}{\rrbracket}}
to be the pair

\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mathsf{ans},\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mathsf{yes},\mathsf{no}$}\mathclose{}{\}}}{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\textstyle\mathsf{yes},\mathsf{no}$}\mathclose{}{\}}}{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mathsf{yes},\mathsf{no}$}\mathclose{}{\}}}{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{yes},\mathsf{no}$}\mathclose{}{\}}}\subseteq\mathscr{C}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mathbf{1}_{\mathscr{C}},\mathsf{ans}$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\textstyle\mathbf{1}_{\mathscr{C}},\mathsf{ans}$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mathbf{1}_{\mathscr{C}},\mathsf{ans}$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathbf{1}_{\mathscr{C}},\mathsf{ans}$}\mathclose{}{]}}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle\mathsf{ans},\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mathsf{yes},\mathsf{no}$}\mathclose{}{\}}}{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\textstyle\mathsf{yes},\mathsf{no}$}\mathclose{}{\}}}{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mathsf{yes},\mathsf{no}$}\mathclose{}{\}}}{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{yes},\mathsf{no}$}\mathclose{}{\}}}\subseteq\mathscr{C}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mathbf{1}_{\mathscr{C}},\mathsf{ans}$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\textstyle\mathbf{1}_{\mathscr{C}},\mathsf{ans}$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mathbf{1}_{\mathscr{C}},\mathsf{ans}$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathbf{1}_{\mathscr{C}},\mathsf{ans}$}\mathclose{}{]}}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mathsf{ans},\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mathsf{yes},\mathsf{no}$}\mathclose{}{\}}}{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\textstyle\mathsf{yes},\mathsf{no}$}\mathclose{}{\}}}{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mathsf{yes},\mathsf{no}$}\mathclose{}{\}}}{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{yes},\mathsf{no}$}\mathclose{}{\}}}\subseteq\mathscr{C}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mathbf{1}_{\mathscr{C}},\mathsf{ans}$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\textstyle\mathbf{1}_{\mathscr{C}},\mathsf{ans}$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mathbf{1}_{\mathscr{C}},\mathsf{ans}$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathbf{1}_{\mathscr{C}},\mathsf{ans}$}\mathclose{}{]}}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{ans},\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mathsf{yes},\mathsf{no}$}\mathclose{}{\}}}{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\textstyle\mathsf{yes},\mathsf{no}$}\mathclose{}{\}}}{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mathsf{yes},\mathsf{no}$}\mathclose{}{\}}}{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{yes},\mathsf{no}$}\mathclose{}{\}}}\subseteq\mathscr{C}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mathbf{1}_{\mathscr{C}},\mathsf{ans}$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\textstyle\mathbf{1}_{\mathscr{C}},\mathsf{ans}$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mathbf{1}_{\mathscr{C}},\mathsf{ans}$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathbf{1}_{\mathscr{C}},\mathsf{ans}$}\mathclose{}{]}}$}\mathclose{}{)}}
.
Then the elements
\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{\llbracket}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mathsf{yes}$}\mathclose{}{\rrbracket}}{\mathopen{}{\llbracket}\hbox{$\textstyle\mathsf{yes}$}\mathclose{}{\rrbracket}}{\mathopen{}{\llbracket}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mathsf{yes}$}\mathclose{}{\rrbracket}}{\mathopen{}{\llbracket}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{yes}$}\mathclose{}{\rrbracket}},\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{\llbracket}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mathsf{no}$}\mathclose{}{\rrbracket}}{\mathopen{}{\llbracket}\hbox{$\textstyle\mathsf{no}$}\mathclose{}{\rrbracket}}{\mathopen{}{\llbracket}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mathsf{no}$}\mathclose{}{\rrbracket}}{\mathopen{}{\llbracket}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{no}$}\mathclose{}{\rrbracket}}
can be defined to be

\mathsf{yes},\mathsf{no}
respectively. The canonicity theorem follows.

Proof 3.2

(Proof of Proposition
21
)
.

Let
\mathbf{1}_{\mathscr{C}}
\mathsf{ans}
a
be a morphism of
\mathscr{C}
; by means
of the cartesian closed section
\mathscr{C}
\mathscr{P}
\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{\llbracket}\hbox{$\displaystyle-$}\mathclose{}{\rrbracket}}{\mathopen{}{\llbracket}\hbox{$\textstyle-$}\mathclose{}{\rrbracket}}{\mathopen{}{\llbracket}\hbox{$\scriptstyle-$}\mathclose{}{\rrbracket}}{\mathopen{}{\llbracket}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle-$}\mathclose{}{\rrbracket}}
of

\mathscr{P}
\mathscr{C}
p
, there exists a morphism

\mathbf{1}_{\mathscr{P}}
\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{\llbracket}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mathsf{ans}$}\mathclose{}{\rrbracket}}{\mathopen{}{\llbracket}\hbox{$\textstyle\mathsf{ans}$}\mathclose{}{\rrbracket}}{\mathopen{}{\llbracket}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mathsf{ans}$}\mathclose{}{\rrbracket}}{\mathopen{}{\llbracket}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{ans}$}\mathclose{}{\rrbracket}}
\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{\llbracket}\hbox{$\displaystyle a$}\mathclose{}{\rrbracket}}{\mathopen{}{\llbracket}\hbox{$\textstyle a$}\mathclose{}{\rrbracket}}{\mathopen{}{\llbracket}\hbox{$\scriptstyle a$}\mathclose{}{\rrbracket}}{\mathopen{}{\llbracket}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle a$}\mathclose{}{\rrbracket}}
such that

p\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{\llbracket}\hbox{$\displaystyle a$}\mathclose{}{\rrbracket}}{\mathopen{}{\llbracket}\hbox{$\textstyle a$}\mathclose{}{\rrbracket}}{\mathopen{}{\llbracket}\hbox{$\scriptstyle a$}\mathclose{}{\rrbracket}}{\mathopen{}{\llbracket}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle a$}\mathclose{}{\rrbracket}}=a
. Unfolding the definition of morphisms in
\mathscr{P}
and
the definition of
\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{\llbracket}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mathsf{ans}$}\mathclose{}{\rrbracket}}{\mathopen{}{\llbracket}\hbox{$\textstyle\mathsf{ans}$}\mathclose{}{\rrbracket}}{\mathopen{}{\llbracket}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mathsf{ans}$}\mathclose{}{\rrbracket}}{\mathopen{}{\llbracket}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{ans}$}\mathclose{}{\rrbracket}}
, this is the same as saying that

a\in\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mathsf{yes},\mathsf{no}$}\mathclose{}{\}}}{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\textstyle\mathsf{yes},\mathsf{no}$}\mathclose{}{\}}}{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mathsf{yes},\mathsf{no}$}\mathclose{}{\}}}{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{yes},\mathsf{no}$}\mathclose{}{\}}}
.

In this paper, we prove a much more sophisticated canonicity theorem and
therefore must change the construction in a few important ways.

(1)

We replace the proof-irrelevant logical predicate interpretation (based
on subsets) with a proof-relevant interpretation (based on families).

(2)

Rather than considering closed terms (
i.e
.
elements of the hom sets

\mathscr{C}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mathbf{1}_{\mathscr{C}},C$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\textstyle\mathbf{1}_{\mathscr{C}},C$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mathbf{1}_{\mathscr{C}},C$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathbf{1}_{\mathscr{C}},C$}\mathclose{}{]}}
), we consider terms relative to purely
cubical contexts
\Psi=\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\displaystyle i:\mathbb{I},\ldots$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\textstyle i:\mathbb{I},\ldots$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\scriptstyle i:\mathbb{I},\ldots$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle i:\mathbb{I},\ldots$}\mathclose{}{]}}
,
i.e
.
elements of any hom sets

\mathscr{C}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\displaystyle\Psi,C$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\textstyle\Psi,C$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\Psi,C$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\Psi,C$}\mathclose{}{]}}
. We require our families (proof-relevant predicates)
to carry a contravariant functorial action for cubical substitutions
\Psi^{\prime}
\Psi
.

The modifications described above are actually parameters to a much more
general construction called Artin gluing. When
\mathscr{C}
is a category and

\mathscr{C}
\mathscr{E}
F
is a functor, the Artin gluing of
\mathscr{C}
along
F
is
defined be the comma category
\mathscr{G}\equiv{\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mathscr{E}$}\mathclose{}{\}}}{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\textstyle\mathscr{E}$}\mathclose{}{\}}}{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mathscr{E}$}\mathclose{}{\}}}{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathscr{E}$}\mathclose{}{\}}}}\downarrow{F}
. It is instructive to
view the gluing as a restriction of the codomain fibration in the case that

\mathscr{E}
has finite limits:

\mathscr{G}
\mathscr{C}
p
\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\Delta}^{1},\mathscr{E}$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\textstyle\boldsymbol{\Delta}^{1},\mathscr{E}$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{\Delta}^{1},\mathscr{E}$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{\Delta}^{1},\mathscr{E}$}\mathclose{}{]}}
\mathscr{E}
\partial_{1}
F

Artin gluing theorems express the relationship between various properties of

\mathscr{C}
and
F
and
\mathscr{E}
to corresponding properties on
\mathscr{G}
. For
instance, if
F
is a binary product preserving functor between cartesian
closed categories, then
\mathscr{G}
is cartesian closed and

\mathscr{G}
\mathscr{C}
p
preserves the cartesian closed structure. Similar
results hold for topoi, which we make use of in this paper.

4.
Functorial semantics of XTT

In Section
2.4
we defined XTT as a signature in Uemura’s logical framework. Following
Uemura
[
Uem19
]
, for the purposes of our canonicity proof we systematically elaborate this
signature to a series of structures on an arbitrary representable map category

\mathbb{T}

[
Uem19
, Theorem 5.17]
.
\mathbb{T}
is a model of XTT precisely
when it admits all of these structures.
We write
\diamond:\mathbb{T}
for the terminal object of
\mathbb{T}
.

Specification 22

(Judgmental structure)
.

The basic judgmental structure of XTT is specified below.

(1)

A representable map
\widetilde{\mathbf{T}}
\mathbf{T}
\boldsymbol{\uptau}
which encodes the collection
of typed elements lying over typed terms; the representability of
\boldsymbol{\uptau}

allows the (abstract) context to be extended by an element
x:A
of a type

A
.

(2)

A representable map
\mathbb{I}
\diamond
, implementing the interval
and its context extension.

(3)

A representable map
\diamond
\mathbb{F}
\boldsymbol{\top}
, implementing the face
formula judgment and its context extension.
\boldsymbol{\top}
is the “true” face
formula. As a map out of the terminal object,
\boldsymbol{\top}
is automatically monomorphic: this means that two proofs of the
same face formula are identical.
∎

Specification 23

(The interval)
.

We require only minimal structure on the interval, the two endpoints

\diamond
\mathbb{I}
0,1
.
∎

Specification 24

(Dimension equality)
.

\mathbb{I}^{2}

We must be careful when specifying disjunction of face formulas; the “true”
disjunction of
\boldsymbol{\top}[\phi]
and
\boldsymbol{\top}[\psi]
ought to be a pushout, but we
don’t expect to have pushouts in
\mathbb{T}

require the ability to “split” on a disjunction in all the syntactic sorts of
our type theory. Instead, we make
\widetilde{\mathbf{T}}
\mathbf{T}
\boldsymbol{\uptau}

think
that this pushout
exists, in a certain sense.

We begin by formulating the “true” disjunction in the free cocompletion

\mathbf{Pr}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mathbb{T}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle\mathbb{T}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mathbb{T}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathbb{T}$}\mathclose{}{)}}

\mathsf{y}_{\mathbb{T}}{\mathbb{F}}
\mathsf{y}_{\mathbb{T}}{\boldsymbol{\top}}

\mathsf{in}_{\lor}\mathrel{\mathrel{\reflectbox{\rotatebox[origin]{90.0}{$\Vdash$}}}}\mathsf{y}_{\mathbb{T}}{\mathbb{F}^{2}}^{*}\mathsf{y}_{\mathbb{T}}{\boldsymbol{\top}}
in
\mathbf{Pr}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mathbb{T}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle\mathbb{T}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mathbb{T}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathbb{T}$}\mathclose{}{)}}_{{/\mathsf{y}_{\mathbb{T}}{\mathbb{F}^{2}}}}
, ensuring that the truth of a face condition may be established by eliminating a disjunction.

(2)

We must have
\mathsf{in}_{\lor}\mathrel{\mathrel{\reflectbox{\rotatebox[origin]{90.0}{$\Vdash$}}}}\mathsf{y}_{\mathbb{T}}{\mathbb{F}^{2}}^{*}\mathsf{y}_{\mathbb{T}}{\boldsymbol{\uptau}}
in
\mathbf{Pr}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mathbb{T}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle\mathbb{T}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mathbb{T}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathbb{T}$}\mathclose{}{)}}_{{/\mathsf{y}_{\mathbb{T}}{\mathbb{F}^{2}}}}
, ensuring that a “matching family” for a term on two disjuncts shall be a term under a disjunction.
∎

Specification 26

(Falsehood)
.

By Specification
24
, we have a map

\diamond
\mathbb{F}
\bot\overset{\textit{def}}{=\joinrel=}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle=$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle=$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle=$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle=$}\mathclose{}{)}}\circ\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\displaystyle 0,1$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\textstyle 0,1$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\scriptstyle 0,1$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle 0,1$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}
. We may
therefore test the truth of this “false” equation:

\bot^{*}\boldsymbol{\top}
\diamond
\boldsymbol{\top}
\mathbb{F}
\bot
\mathbf{Sub}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mathbb{T}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle\mathbb{T}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mathbb{T}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathbb{T}$}\mathclose{}{)}}
\mathbb{T}

(0)

There is a universal comparison map

\varnothing
\mathsf{y}_{\mathbb{T}}{\bot^{*}\boldsymbol{\top}}
\mathsf{in}_{\bot}
in

\mathbf{Pr}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mathbb{T}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle\mathbb{T}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mathbb{T}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathbb{T}$}\mathclose{}{)}}
given by the universal property of the initial object; to
support the “elimination rule” of the inconsistent face condition, then, we
require orthogonalities
\mathsf{in}_{\bot}\mathrel{\mathrel{\reflectbox{\rotatebox[origin]{90.0}{$\Vdash$}}}}\mathsf{y}_{\mathbb{T}}{\boldsymbol{\top}}
and

\mathsf{in}_{\bot}\mathrel{\mathrel{\reflectbox{\rotatebox[origin]{90.0}{$\Vdash$}}}}\mathsf{y}_{\mathbb{T}}{\boldsymbol{\uptau}}
in
\mathbf{Pr}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mathbb{T}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle\mathbb{T}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mathbb{T}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathbb{T}$}\mathclose{}{)}}
.
∎

The following notation will often be used in the internal language of
\mathbb{T}
.

{nota}

[Restriction to a partial element]
Let
\phi:\mathbb{F}
be a face condition,
A:\mathbf{T}
a type, and
a:\boldsymbol{\top}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\displaystyle\phi$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\textstyle\phi$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\phi$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\phi$}\mathclose{}{]}}\Rightarrow\boldsymbol{\uptau}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\displaystyle A$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\textstyle A$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\scriptstyle A$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle A$}\mathclose{}{]}}
a partial element; we write

\boldsymbol{\uptau}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\displaystyle A\mid\phi\to a$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\textstyle A\mid\phi\to a$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\scriptstyle A\mid\phi\to a$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle A\mid\phi\to a$}\mathclose{}{]}}
for the collection of elements of
A
which
restrict to
a
on
\phi
,
i.e
.
the elements
a^{\prime}:\boldsymbol{\uptau}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\displaystyle A$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\textstyle A$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\scriptstyle A$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle A$}\mathclose{}{]}}
where

\lambda\_.a^{\prime}=a:\boldsymbol{\top}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\displaystyle\phi$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\textstyle\phi$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\phi$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\phi$}\mathclose{}{]}}\Rightarrow A
.
∎

{nota}

[The boundary of a dimension]
We will write
\partial\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle r$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle r$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle r$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle r$}\mathclose{}{)}}:\mathbb{F}
for the
boundary
of a dimension

r:\mathbb{I}
, defined as the disjunction
\partial\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle r$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle r$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle r$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle r$}\mathclose{}{)}}\overset{\textit{def}}{=\joinrel=}(r=0)\lor(r=1)
.
∎

The boundary of a dimension will be used in specifying the closure under

path types
.

Specification 29

(Closure under connectives)
.

We will require that typing judgment
\widetilde{\mathbf{T}}
\mathbf{T}
\boldsymbol{\uptau}
is closed under dependent
sum, dependent product, and dependent
path
types. We first express the
generic map underlying each connective, and then force it to be representable.

We will add a type of
booleans
; as usual in type theory, the boolean
type is
not
the coproduct of the point with itself, but a weak version
thereof. The simplest way to specify a weak coproduct is by means of a left
lifting structure (Definition
3.3
) internal to the

free cocompletion

\mathbf{Pr}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mathbb{T}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle\mathbb{T}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mathbb{T}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathbb{T}$}\mathclose{}{)}}
of
\mathbb{T}
.

Remark 32
.

We may unravel Specification
31
into the language of

\mathbb{T}
using Lemma
20
. First, the morphism
i_{\mathrm{bool}}

corresponds to exactly two introduction forms

\diamond
\mathrm{bool}^{*}\boldsymbol{\uptau}
\mathsf{tt},\mathsf{ff}
in
\mathbb{T}
; the left lifting
structure
\mathsf{ind}_{\mathrm{bool}}
amounts to a choice of section for the
cartesian gap map of the following canonical square:

\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{\llbracket}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mathrm{bool}^{*}\boldsymbol{\uptau},\widetilde{\mathbf{T}}$}\mathclose{}{\rrbracket}}{\mathopen{}{\llbracket}\hbox{$\textstyle\mathrm{bool}^{*}\boldsymbol{\uptau},\widetilde{\mathbf{T}}$}\mathclose{}{\rrbracket}}{\mathopen{}{\llbracket}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mathrm{bool}^{*}\boldsymbol{\uptau},\widetilde{\mathbf{T}}$}\mathclose{}{\rrbracket}}{\mathopen{}{\llbracket}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{bool}^{*}\boldsymbol{\uptau},\widetilde{\mathbf{T}}$}\mathclose{}{\rrbracket}}

Specification 35

(Type-case)
.

The type-case construct of XTT’s closed universe is implemented by a left
lifting structure. First, we define the following coproduct in the free
cocompletion
\mathbf{Pr}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mathbb{T}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle\mathbb{T}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mathbb{T}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathbb{T}$}\mathclose{}{)}}
:

\mathfrak{F}_{\mathbf{set}}\overset{\textit{def}}{=\joinrel=}\mathsf{y}_{\mathbb{T}}{\mathbf{set}^{\Sigma}}+\mathsf{y}_{\mathbb{T}}{\mathbf{set}^{\Pi}}+\mathsf{y}_{\mathbb{T}}{\mathbf{set}^{\mathrm{P}}}+\mathsf{y}_{\mathbb{T}}{\diamond}

The codes for each type constructor can be arranged into an algebra

\mathfrak{F}_{\mathbf{set}}
\mathsf{y}_{\mathbb{T}}{\mathbf{set}}
\alpha_{\mathbf{set}}
:

\mathfrak{F}_{\mathbf{set}}
\mathsf{y}_{\mathbb{T}}{\mathbf{set}}
\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mathsf{y}_{\mathbb{T}}{\widehat{\mathsf{sg}}}\mid\mathsf{y}_{\mathbb{T}}{\widehat{\mathsf{pi}}}\mid\mathsf{y}_{\mathbb{T}}{\widehat{\mathsf{path}}}\mid\mathsf{y}_{\mathbb{T}}{\widehat{\mathsf{bool}}}$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\textstyle\mathsf{y}_{\mathbb{T}}{\widehat{\mathsf{sg}}}\mid\mathsf{y}_{\mathbb{T}}{\widehat{\mathsf{pi}}}\mid\mathsf{y}_{\mathbb{T}}{\widehat{\mathsf{path}}}\mid\mathsf{y}_{\mathbb{T}}{\widehat{\mathsf{bool}}}$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mathsf{y}_{\mathbb{T}}{\widehat{\mathsf{sg}}}\mid\mathsf{y}_{\mathbb{T}}{\widehat{\mathsf{pi}}}\mid\mathsf{y}_{\mathbb{T}}{\widehat{\mathsf{path}}}\mid\mathsf{y}_{\mathbb{T}}{\widehat{\mathsf{bool}}}$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{y}_{\mathbb{T}}{\widehat{\mathsf{sg}}}\mid\mathsf{y}_{\mathbb{T}}{\widehat{\mathsf{pi}}}\mid\mathsf{y}_{\mathbb{T}}{\widehat{\mathsf{path}}}\mid\mathsf{y}_{\mathbb{T}}{\widehat{\mathsf{bool}}}$}\mathclose{}{]}}

We then require a left lifting structure
\mathsf{case}_{\mathbf{set}}:\alpha_{\mathbf{set}}\pitchfork\mathsf{y}_{\mathbb{T}}{\boldsymbol{\uptau}}
, which provides solutions to lifting problems of the following shape:

The types encoded by XTT’s closed universe must be “fibrant” in the sense
that they support transport along paths and composition of paths. We will
express these as two separate left lifting structures, with suitable
compatibility laws.

Proof 4.1
.

By boundary separation, pivoting on
s:\mathbb{I}
.

4.2.
Summary

We have expressed the necessary and sufficient conditions on a representable
map category to be an algebra for the XTT language. From now on, we will take

\mathbb{T}
to be the
smallest
representable map category satisfying the
present specification, hence
\mathbb{T}
is the syntactic category of XTT. The
existence of such a representable map category follows from Proposition 5.16 of
[
Uem19
]
. A model of XTT in a representable map category
\mathscr{C}
is
then precisely a functor
\mathbb{T}
\mathbf{DF}_{\mathscr{C}}
\mathscr{M}_{\mathscr{C}}
.

5.
Cubical computability structures

In this section we develop the building blocks of the canonicity proof for XTT. While
eventually these shall be applied to the initial model, we work with an arbitrary
model
\mathbb{T}
\mathbf{DF}_{\mathscr{C}}
\mathscr{M}_{\mathscr{C}}
.

In 2015, Awodey suggested the idea of gluing along a
cubical nerve
like
Construction
45
to develop the metatheory of cubical type
theory; to many researchers, it seemed as though Huber’s operational proof of
canonicity for cubical type theory
[
Hub18
]
could be reconstructed in
a mathematical way. Since then, Awodey and Fiore have used this cubical gluing
technique to study a version of intensional type theory with an interval in
unpublished joint work; in 2019, the present authors applied cubical gluing to
prove canonicity for an earlier version of
XTT
[
SAG19
]
.

Lemma 46
.

The cubical nerve is
flat
.

Proof 5.1
.

By Diaconescu’s theorem
[
Bor10
]

,
whose objects are “cubically computable contexts” and whose morphisms are natural transformations
of cubical sets that are tracked by substitutions from the model
\mathscr{M}_{\mathscr{C}}
. Intuitively, a glued
context is a pair of a syntactic context with a (proof-relevant) Kripke predicate indexed in
dimension variable contexts. By analogy with
[
Tai67
]
, we regard the image of these
predicates as the
computable
closing substitutions of contexts. Because glued substitutions
are commuting squares, they automatically send computable elements to computable elements; the top
map of such a square sends computability witnesses to computability witnesses.

By defining a model of XTT in this category (
i.e
.
collections of glued types and elements closed
under the rules), we obtain a categorical version of a logical relations model of XTT. Our
categorical perspective immediately offers some advantages over “free-style” logical relations for
dependent type theory—much of the indexing can be moved behind categorical abstractions, and
certain results become automatic, such as computable substitutions being closed under composition.
By choosing certain predicates appropriately, we can moreover ensure that the computable elements of
boolean types are precisely
\mathsf{tt}
and
\mathsf{ff}
,
etc
.

This is the perspective pursued in previous work on gluing for strict type
theory
[
SAG19
,
KHS19
,
CHS19
,
GKNB20
]
;
in recent joint work, the first two authors of this paper have argued that it
is considerably simpler to first glue over
\mathbf{DF}_{\mathscr{C}}
rather than
\mathscr{C}
,
and then restrict further to
\mathscr{C}
by pulling back along

\mathscr{C}
\mathbf{DF}_{\mathscr{C}}
\mathsf{y}_{\mathscr{C}}

[
SA20
]
.

Following
[

]

, being a Grothendieck logos
[
AGV72
]
.
The resulting two-step gluing process amounts to enlarging the collection of
computability structures to ones that lie over arbitrary discrete fibrations

X:\mathbf{DF}_{\mathscr{C}}
, in addition to the familiar ones that lie directly over
contexts
\Gamma:\mathscr{C}
.
Computability structures lying over a context
\Gamma:\mathscr{C}
will be referred
to as “compact”; the fundamental example of a computability structure which is
not compact is the computability structure of computable types, lying over the
non-representable discrete fibration
\mathbf{T}_{\mathscr{C}}:\mathbf{DF}_{\mathscr{C}}
.

The general computability structures are connected to a
model
of type
theory (which must take place in discrete fibrations over
compact

computability structures) via a nerve–realization adjunction. The nerve functor
\mathscr{G}
\mathbf{DF}_{\mathscr{G}_{\mathsf{K}}}
is fully faithful and even locally
cartesian closed, and may therefore be used to transform general computability
families into constituents of a model of type theory over
\mathscr{G}_{\mathsf{K}}
which are
otherwise vastly more difficult to compute.

{defi}

An object
X:\mathscr{G}
is
compact
when it lies in the essential image of
\mathsf{K}
;
equivalently, when
\boldsymbol{j}^{*}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle X$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle X$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle X$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle X$}\mathclose{}{)}}:\mathbf{DF}_{\mathscr{C}}
is representable.
∎

We may impose the structure of a representable map category on
\mathscr{G}
, based
on generalizing the notion of compactness from objects to families.

5.2.
Nerve and realization

A computability model of XTT is given by a representable map functor

\mathbb{T}
\mathbf{DF}_{\mathscr{G}_{\mathsf{K}}}
\mathscr{M}_{\mathscr{G}_{\mathsf{K}}}
; in particular, we must
construct a natural model in
\mathbf{DF}_{\mathscr{G}_{\mathsf{K}}}
which is closed under all the
connectives of XTT and its universe of Bishop sets. These objects are, however,
particularly difficult to construct from the perspective of discrete
fibrations or presheaves; in previous work, it has accordingly been necessary to construct
the constitutents of the computability model at the level of
sets
[
SAG19
,
Coq19
,
KHS19
]
,
manually quantifying over computable contexts and computable substitutions.

In recent work, Sterling and Angiuli have shown that it is simpler to construct
these objects
internally
to the logos
\mathscr{G}
of general computability
structures, and then transfer them in a single motion to
\mathbf{DF}_{\mathscr{G}_{\mathsf{K}}}
. This
is accomplished by means of a
nerve
functor

\mathscr{G}
\mathbf{DF}_{\mathscr{G}_{\mathsf{K}}}
\mathsf{N}_{\mathsf{K}}
which, by virtue of the density of

\mathscr{G}_{\mathsf{K}}
\mathscr{G}
\mathsf{K}
(Theorem
5.1
), is
not only fully faithful but also locally cartesian closed. Crucially,
\mathsf{N}_{\mathsf{K}}

will also turn out to be a representable map functor.

Lemma 51

(Realization)
.

The nerve functor has a left adjoint
\mathbf{DF}_{\mathscr{G}_{\mathsf{K}}}
\mathscr{G}
\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{\lvert}\hbox{$\displaystyle-$}\mathclose{}{\rvert}}{\mathopen{}{\lvert}\hbox{$\textstyle-$}\mathclose{}{\rvert}}{\mathopen{}{\lvert}\hbox{$\scriptstyle-$}\mathclose{}{\rvert}}{\mathopen{}{\lvert}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle-$}\mathclose{}{\rvert}}_{\mathsf{K}}
,
the
realization
of a discrete fibration on compact computability
structures; consequently,
\mathsf{N}_{\mathsf{K}}
preserves small limits.

Proof 5.6
.

The realization functor is obtained by left Kan extension:

\mathscr{G}_{\mathsf{K}}
\mathbf{DF}_{\mathscr{G}_{\mathsf{K}}}
\mathscr{G}
\mathsf{K}
\mathsf{y}_{\mathscr{G}_{\mathsf{K}}}
\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{\lvert}\hbox{$\displaystyle-$}\mathclose{}{\rvert}}{\mathopen{}{\lvert}\hbox{$\textstyle-$}\mathclose{}{\rvert}}{\mathopen{}{\lvert}\hbox{$\scriptstyle-$}\mathclose{}{\rvert}}{\mathopen{}{\lvert}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle-$}\mathclose{}{\rvert}}_{\mathsf{K}}
\Downarrow

The realization of a specific discrete fibration may be computed as a coend,
using the general formula for pointwise Kan extensions. Letting
F:\mathbf{DF}_{\mathscr{G}_{\mathsf{K}}}
, we calculate:

\displaystyle\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{\lvert}\hbox{$\displaystyle F$}\mathclose{}{\rvert}}{\mathopen{}{\lvert}\hbox{$\textstyle F$}\mathclose{}{\rvert}}{\mathopen{}{\lvert}\hbox{$\scriptstyle F$}\mathclose{}{\rvert}}{\mathopen{}{\lvert}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle F$}\mathclose{}{\rvert}}_{\mathsf{K}}

\displaystyle\cong\mathchoice{\mathopen{\mathchoice{\big(}{\big(}{\big(}{(}}\hbox{$\displaystyle\operatorname{Lan}_{\mathsf{y}_{\mathscr{G}_{\mathsf{K}}}}{\mathsf{K}}$}\mathclose{\mathchoice{\big)}{\big)}{\big)}{)}}}{\mathopen{\mathchoice{\big(}{\big(}{\big(}{(}}\hbox{$\textstyle\operatorname{Lan}_{\mathsf{y}_{\mathscr{G}_{\mathsf{K}}}}{\mathsf{K}}$}\mathclose{\mathchoice{\big)}{\big)}{\big)}{)}}}{\mathopen{\mathchoice{\big(}{\big(}{\big(}{(}}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\operatorname{Lan}_{\mathsf{y}_{\mathscr{G}_{\mathsf{K}}}}{\mathsf{K}}$}\mathclose{\mathchoice{\big)}{\big)}{\big)}{)}}}{\mathopen{\mathchoice{\big(}{\big(}{\big(}{(}}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\operatorname{Lan}_{\mathsf{y}_{\mathscr{G}_{\mathsf{K}}}}{\mathsf{K}}$}\mathclose{\mathchoice{\big)}{\big)}{\big)}{)}}}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle F$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle F$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle F$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle F$}\mathclose{}{)}}

\displaystyle\cong{\textstyle\int}^{\Gamma:\mathscr{G}_{\mathsf{K}}}{\mathbf{DF}_{\mathscr{G}_{\mathsf{K}}}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mathsf{y}_{\mathscr{G}_{\mathsf{K}}}{\Gamma},F$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\textstyle\mathsf{y}_{\mathscr{G}_{\mathsf{K}}}{\Gamma},F$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mathsf{y}_{\mathscr{G}_{\mathsf{K}}}{\Gamma},F$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{y}_{\mathscr{G}_{\mathsf{K}}}{\Gamma},F$}\mathclose{}{]}}\cdot\mathsf{K}{\Gamma}}

\displaystyle\cong{\textstyle\int}^{\Gamma:\mathscr{G}_{\mathsf{K}}}{F_{\Gamma}\cdot\mathsf{K}{\Gamma}}

Writing
\mathscr{G}_{\mathsf{K}}^{\mathsf{op}}
\mathbf{Set}
F_{\bullet}
for the presheaf
corresponding to the discrete fibration
F
, we may package the computation of

F
’s realization in terms of the tensor calculus of functors:

\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{\lvert}\hbox{$\displaystyle F$}\mathclose{}{\rvert}}{\mathopen{}{\lvert}\hbox{$\textstyle F$}\mathclose{}{\rvert}}{\mathopen{}{\lvert}\hbox{$\scriptstyle F$}\mathclose{}{\rvert}}{\mathopen{}{\lvert}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle F$}\mathclose{}{\rvert}}_{\mathsf{K}}\cong F_{\bullet}\otimes_{\mathscr{G}_{\mathsf{K}}}\mathsf{K}

(0)

From Lemma
52
below, we can see that the nerve exhibits a true
“Yoneda embedding” of general computability structures into discrete
fibrations.

Lemma 52
.

The nerve functor
\mathscr{G}
\mathbf{DF}_{\mathscr{G}_{\mathsf{K}}}
\mathsf{N}_{\mathsf{K}}
is fully faithful.

Proof 5.7
.

This is equivalent to the density of the inclusion
\mathsf{K}
.

Lemma 53

(Equivalent subcategories)
.

The nerve–realization adjunction
\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{\lvert}\hbox{$\displaystyle-$}\mathclose{}{\rvert}}{\mathopen{}{\lvert}\hbox{$\textstyle-$}\mathclose{}{\rvert}}{\mathopen{}{\lvert}\hbox{$\scriptstyle-$}\mathclose{}{\rvert}}{\mathopen{}{\lvert}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle-$}\mathclose{}{\rvert}}_{\mathsf{K}}\dashv\mathsf{N}_{\mathsf{K}}
restricts to an equivalence (of categories) between the subcategories of generating objects (compact computability
structures and representable presheaves respectively).

Proof 5.8
.

We first check that the nerve of any compact computability structure
X\cong\mathsf{K}{\Gamma}
is a representable discrete fibration. It suffices to
compute in terms of the corresponding presheaves,

\mathsf{N}_{\mathsf{K}}{\mathsf{K}{\Gamma}}_{\bullet}\cong\mathscr{G}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mathsf{K}{\bullet},\mathsf{K}{\Gamma}$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\textstyle\mathsf{K}{\bullet},\mathsf{K}{\Gamma}$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mathsf{K}{\bullet},\mathsf{K}{\Gamma}$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{K}{\bullet},\mathsf{K}{\Gamma}$}\mathclose{}{]}}\cong\mathscr{G}_{\mathsf{K}}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\displaystyle\bullet,\Gamma$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\textstyle\bullet,\Gamma$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\bullet,\Gamma$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\bullet,\Gamma$}\mathclose{}{]}}\cong\mathsf{y}_{\mathscr{G}_{\mathsf{K}}}{\Gamma}\cong\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mathsf{y}_{\mathscr{G}_{\mathsf{K}}}{\Gamma}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle\mathsf{y}_{\mathscr{G}_{\mathsf{K}}}{\Gamma}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mathsf{y}_{\mathscr{G}_{\mathsf{K}}}{\Gamma}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{y}_{\mathscr{G}_{\mathsf{K}}}{\Gamma}$}\mathclose{}{)}}_{\bullet}
.
Therefore, we have
\mathsf{N}_{\mathsf{K}}{\mathsf{K}{\Gamma}}\cong\mathsf{y}_{\mathscr{G}_{\mathsf{K}}}{\Gamma}
.
Next, we check that the realization of any representable discrete fibration

F\cong\mathsf{y}_{\mathscr{G}_{\mathsf{K}}}{\Gamma}
is compact; by the above, we have
\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{\lvert}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mathsf{y}_{\mathscr{G}_{\mathsf{K}}}{\Gamma}$}\mathclose{}{\rvert}}{\mathopen{}{\lvert}\hbox{$\textstyle\mathsf{y}_{\mathscr{G}_{\mathsf{K}}}{\Gamma}$}\mathclose{}{\rvert}}{\mathopen{}{\lvert}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mathsf{y}_{\mathscr{G}_{\mathsf{K}}}{\Gamma}$}\mathclose{}{\rvert}}{\mathopen{}{\lvert}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{y}_{\mathscr{G}_{\mathsf{K}}}{\Gamma}$}\mathclose{}{\rvert}}_{\mathsf{K}}\cong\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{\lvert}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mathsf{N}_{\mathsf{K}}{\mathsf{K}{\Gamma}}$}\mathclose{}{\rvert}}{\mathopen{}{\lvert}\hbox{$\textstyle\mathsf{N}_{\mathsf{K}}{\mathsf{K}{\Gamma}}$}\mathclose{}{\rvert}}{\mathopen{}{\lvert}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mathsf{N}_{\mathsf{K}}{\mathsf{K}{\Gamma}}$}\mathclose{}{\rvert}}{\mathopen{}{\lvert}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{N}_{\mathsf{K}}{\mathsf{K}{\Gamma}}$}\mathclose{}{\rvert}}_{\mathsf{K}}
; because the nerve is fully faithful
(Lemma
52
), the counit to the adjunction
\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{\lvert}\hbox{$\displaystyle-$}\mathclose{}{\rvert}}{\mathopen{}{\lvert}\hbox{$\textstyle-$}\mathclose{}{\rvert}}{\mathopen{}{\lvert}\hbox{$\scriptstyle-$}\mathclose{}{\rvert}}{\mathopen{}{\lvert}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle-$}\mathclose{}{\rvert}}_{\mathsf{K}}\dashv\mathsf{N}_{\mathsf{K}}

is an isomorphism, so we further have
\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{\lvert}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mathsf{y}_{\mathscr{G}_{\mathsf{K}}}{\Gamma}$}\mathclose{}{\rvert}}{\mathopen{}{\lvert}\hbox{$\textstyle\mathsf{y}_{\mathscr{G}_{\mathsf{K}}}{\Gamma}$}\mathclose{}{\rvert}}{\mathopen{}{\lvert}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mathsf{y}_{\mathscr{G}_{\mathsf{K}}}{\Gamma}$}\mathclose{}{\rvert}}{\mathopen{}{\lvert}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{y}_{\mathscr{G}_{\mathsf{K}}}{\Gamma}$}\mathclose{}{\rvert}}_{\mathsf{K}}\cong\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{\lvert}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mathsf{N}_{\mathsf{K}}{\mathsf{K}{\Gamma}}$}\mathclose{}{\rvert}}{\mathopen{}{\lvert}\hbox{$\textstyle\mathsf{N}_{\mathsf{K}}{\mathsf{K}{\Gamma}}$}\mathclose{}{\rvert}}{\mathopen{}{\lvert}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mathsf{N}_{\mathsf{K}}{\mathsf{K}{\Gamma}}$}\mathclose{}{\rvert}}{\mathopen{}{\lvert}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{N}_{\mathsf{K}}{\mathsf{K}{\Gamma}}$}\mathclose{}{\rvert}}_{\mathsf{K}}\cong\mathsf{K}{\Gamma}
.

We have shown that the nerve–realization adjunction restricts to a pair of functors between subcategories. It is easy to see that this is in fact an
equivalence, since we have shown that
\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{\lvert}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mathsf{N}_{\mathsf{K}}{\mathsf{K}{\Gamma}}$}\mathclose{}{\rvert}}{\mathopen{}{\lvert}\hbox{$\textstyle\mathsf{N}_{\mathsf{K}}{\mathsf{K}{\Gamma}}$}\mathclose{}{\rvert}}{\mathopen{}{\lvert}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mathsf{N}_{\mathsf{K}}{\mathsf{K}{\Gamma}}$}\mathclose{}{\rvert}}{\mathopen{}{\lvert}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{N}_{\mathsf{K}}{\mathsf{K}{\Gamma}}$}\mathclose{}{\rvert}}_{\mathsf{K}}\cong\mathsf{K}{\Gamma}
and
\mathsf{N}_{\mathsf{K}}{\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{\lvert}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mathsf{y}_{\mathscr{G}_{\mathsf{K}}}{\Gamma}$}\mathclose{}{\rvert}}{\mathopen{}{\lvert}\hbox{$\textstyle\mathsf{y}_{\mathscr{G}_{\mathsf{K}}}{\Gamma}$}\mathclose{}{\rvert}}{\mathopen{}{\lvert}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mathsf{y}_{\mathscr{G}_{\mathsf{K}}}{\Gamma}$}\mathclose{}{\rvert}}{\mathopen{}{\lvert}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{y}_{\mathscr{G}_{\mathsf{K}}}{\Gamma}$}\mathclose{}{\rvert}}_{\mathsf{K}}}\cong\mathsf{N}_{\mathsf{K}}{\mathsf{K}{\Gamma}}\cong\mathsf{y}_{\mathscr{G}_{\mathsf{K}}}{\Gamma}
.

To establish the behavior of the nerve on pushforwards, it will be useful to
choose a good dense subcategory of each slice
\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mathbf{DF}_{\mathscr{G}_{\mathsf{K}}}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle\mathbf{DF}_{\mathscr{G}_{\mathsf{K}}}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mathbf{DF}_{\mathscr{G}_{\mathsf{K}}}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathbf{DF}_{\mathscr{G}_{\mathsf{K}}}$}\mathclose{}{)}}_{{/F}}
.

Remark 54
.

First we recall that in presheaves, each slice

\mathbf{Pr}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mathscr{G}_{\mathsf{K}}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle\mathscr{G}_{\mathsf{K}}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mathscr{G}_{\mathsf{K}}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathscr{G}_{\mathsf{K}}$}\mathclose{}{)}}_{{/F_{\bullet}}}
may be reconstructed equivalently as the
category of presheaves
\mathbf{Pr}\mathchoice{\mathopen{\mathchoice{\big(}{\big(}{\big(}{(}}\hbox{$\displaystyle\int\!F_{\bullet}$}\mathclose{\mathchoice{\big)}{\big)}{\big)}{)}}}{\mathopen{\mathchoice{\big(}{\big(}{\big(}{(}}\hbox{$\textstyle\int\!F_{\bullet}$}\mathclose{\mathchoice{\big)}{\big)}{\big)}{)}}}{\mathopen{\mathchoice{\big(}{\big(}{\big(}{(}}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\int\!F_{\bullet}$}\mathclose{\mathchoice{\big)}{\big)}{\big)}{)}}}{\mathopen{\mathchoice{\big(}{\big(}{\big(}{(}}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\int\!F_{\bullet}$}\mathclose{\mathchoice{\big)}{\big)}{\big)}{)}}}=\mathbf{Pr}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle F$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle F$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle F$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle F$}\mathclose{}{)}}
on the
total category of
F
; therefore, by the Yoneda lemma, each slice

\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mathbf{DF}_{\mathscr{G}_{\mathsf{K}}}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle\mathbf{DF}_{\mathscr{G}_{\mathsf{K}}}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mathbf{DF}_{\mathscr{G}_{\mathsf{K}}}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathbf{DF}_{\mathscr{G}_{\mathsf{K}}}$}\mathclose{}{)}}_{{/F}}
is densely generated by the functor

F
\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mathbf{DF}_{\mathscr{G}_{\mathsf{K}}}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle\mathbf{DF}_{\mathscr{G}_{\mathsf{K}}}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mathbf{DF}_{\mathscr{G}_{\mathsf{K}}}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathbf{DF}_{\mathscr{G}_{\mathsf{K}}}$}\mathclose{}{)}}_{{/F}}
which sends every element
x\in F_{\Gamma}

to the corresponding map
\mathsf{y}_{\mathscr{G}_{\mathsf{K}}}{\Gamma}
F
x
.

Furthermore, by Lemma
53
each generating object

\mathsf{y}_{\mathscr{G}_{\mathsf{K}}}{\Gamma}
F
may be written equivalently as

\mathsf{N}_{\mathsf{K}}{\mathsf{K}{\Gamma}}
F
. If
F=\mathsf{N}_{\mathsf{K}}{X}
, we may observe that
the slice
\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mathbf{DF}_{\mathscr{G}_{\mathsf{K}}}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle\mathbf{DF}_{\mathscr{G}_{\mathsf{K}}}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mathbf{DF}_{\mathscr{G}_{\mathsf{K}}}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathbf{DF}_{\mathscr{G}_{\mathsf{K}}}$}\mathclose{}{)}}_{{/F}}
is in fact densely generated by the comma
category
{\mathsf{K}}\downarrow{\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\displaystyle X$}\mathclose{}{\}}}{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\textstyle X$}\mathclose{}{\}}}{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\scriptstyle X$}\mathclose{}{\}}}{\mathopen{}{\{}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle X$}\mathclose{}{\}}}}
under the functor which sends each

\mathsf{K}{\Gamma}
X
x
to
\mathsf{N}_{\mathsf{K}}{x}:\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mathbf{DF}_{\mathscr{G}_{\mathsf{K}}}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle\mathbf{DF}_{\mathscr{G}_{\mathsf{K}}}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mathbf{DF}_{\mathscr{G}_{\mathsf{K}}}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathbf{DF}_{\mathscr{G}_{\mathsf{K}}}$}\mathclose{}{)}}_{{/F}}
, a
direct consequence of the fully faithfulness of the nerve
(Lemma
52
).
∎

f
\ulcorner x\urcorner

(Disjunction elimination / truth)
.

The glued disjunction satisfies the internal orthogonality condition with
respect to
\mathscr{G}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\top}$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\textstyle\boldsymbol{\top}$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{\top}$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{\top}$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}

Construction 74

(Booleans)
.

73
, there exists some

\mathscr{G}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\displaystyle\diamond$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\textstyle\diamond$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\diamond$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\diamond$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}

\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{\lceil}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mathrm{bool}^{*}\boldsymbol{\uptau}$}\mathclose{}{\rceil}}{\mathopen{}{\lceil}\hbox{$\textstyle\mathrm{bool}^{*}\boldsymbol{\uptau}$}\mathclose{}{\rceil}}{\mathopen{}{\lceil}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mathrm{bool}^{*}\boldsymbol{\uptau}$}\mathclose{}{\rceil}}{\mathopen{}{\lceil}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{bool}^{*}\boldsymbol{\uptau}$}\mathclose{}{\rceil}}
for

lying over a characteristic map for the object

\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mathrm{bool}^{*}\boldsymbol{\uptau}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle\mathrm{bool}^{*}\boldsymbol{\uptau}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mathrm{bool}^{*}\boldsymbol{\uptau}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{bool}^{*}\boldsymbol{\uptau}$}\mathclose{}{)}}_{\mathscr{C}}

not

.

6.4.
Summary

By means of the foregoing constructions, we have defined a functorial
interpretation
\mathscr{G}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\displaystyle-$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\textstyle-$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\scriptstyle-$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle-$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}
of XTT into a glued logos
\mathscr{G}
lying over

\mathbf{DF}_{\mathscr{C}}
for an arbitrary XTT-model
\mathscr{M}_{\mathscr{C}}
. In
Section
7
, we will reassamble this data into a gluing model

\mathscr{M}_{\mathscr{G}_{\mathsf{K}}}
equipped with a structure map

\mathscr{M}_{\mathscr{G}_{\mathsf{K}}}
\mathscr{M}_{\mathscr{C}}
that can be used to prove canonicity.

7.
Canonicity for XTT

In Section
5
, we introduced the logos
\mathscr{G}
of
computability structures
,
along with a representable map functor
\mathbb{T}
\mathscr{G}
\mathscr{G}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\displaystyle-$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\textstyle-$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\scriptstyle-$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle-$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}
. These constructions contain
the essence of the proof of canonicity for XTT, but in order to complete the proof we must assemble

\mathscr{G}
and
\mathscr{G}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\displaystyle-$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\textstyle-$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\scriptstyle-$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle-$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}
into a model of
\mathbb{T}
equipped with a morphism to
\mathscr{M}_{\mathscr{C}}
. In this
section, we construct this
gluing model
of XTT and prove the following canonicity theorem:

{restatable*}
[Canonicity]thmCanonicityThm
Given a closed term
M:\mathrm{bool}
, either
M=\mathsf{tt}
or
M=\mathsf{ff}
.

7.1.
The canonicity model of XTT

Recall from Section
4
that a model of
\mathbb{T}
is a category with a
terminal object
\mathscr{C}
paired with a representable map functor

\mathbb{T}
\mathbf{DF}_{\mathscr{C}}
\mathscr{M}_{\mathscr{C}}
. The category of computability structures
\mathscr{G}
is not a
category of discrete fibrations, and therefore we cannot directly take
\mathscr{G},\mathscr{G}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\displaystyle-$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\textstyle-$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\scriptstyle-$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}{\mathopen{}{\langle}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle-$}\mathclose{}{\rangle}}
as the gluing
model.
Instead, following
[
SA20
]
we will shift to working with discrete fibrations on

compact
computability structures
\mathbf{DF}_{\mathscr{G}_{\mathsf{K}}}
and use the representable map functor

\mathscr{G}
\mathbf{DF}_{\mathscr{G}_{\mathsf{K}}}
\mathsf{N}_{\mathsf{K}}
to uniformly transfer the computability structures from
Section
5
from
\mathscr{G}
to
\mathbf{DF}_{\mathscr{G}_{\mathsf{K}}}
.

Corollary 84
.

The natural transformation
\mathscr{M}_{\boldsymbol{j}^{*}_{\mathsf{K}}}
from Construction
82
is a morphism of models.
∎

7.2.
The canonicity theorem

Having constructed the gluing model and the projection onto
\mathscr{M}_{\mathscr{C}}
, we are now in a position
to prove canonicity. First, we stop considering an arbitrary model
\mathscr{M}_{\mathscr{C}}
and work
exclusively with
\mathscr{M}_{\mathscr{I}}
, the bi-initial model of
\mathbb{T}

(Theorem
18
). Bi-initiality ensures that there is a morphism

\mathscr{M}_{\mathscr{I}}
\mathscr{M}_{\mathscr{G}_{\mathsf{K}}}
i_{\mathscr{G}_{\mathsf{K}}}
and, because
\mathbf{id}_{\mathscr{M}_{\mathscr{I}}}
and

\mathscr{M}_{\boldsymbol{j}^{*}_{\mathsf{K}}}\circ\mathscr{M}_{i_{\mathscr{G}_{\mathsf{K}}}}
are both objects of

\mathbf{Mod}_{\mathbb{T}}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mathscr{M}_{\mathscr{I}},\mathscr{M}_{\mathscr{I}}$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\textstyle\mathscr{M}_{\mathscr{I}},\mathscr{M}_{\mathscr{I}}$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mathscr{M}_{\mathscr{I}},\mathscr{M}_{\mathscr{I}}$}\mathclose{}{]}}{\mathopen{}{[}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathscr{M}_{\mathscr{I}},\mathscr{M}_{\mathscr{I}}$}\mathclose{}{]}}
, there is a unique invertible 2-morphism

\mathbf{id}_{\mathscr{M}_{\mathscr{I}}}
\mathscr{M}_{\boldsymbol{j}^{*}_{\mathsf{K}}}\circ\mathscr{M}_{i_{\mathscr{G}_{\mathsf{K}}}}
\boldsymbol{\iota}
.

In prior presentations of gluing with strict
homomorphisms
[
SAG19
,
KHS19
,
CHS19
,
GKNB20
]
,

\mathscr{M}_{\mathscr{I}}
was initial in the
1-categorical
sense, so

\mathbf{id}_{\mathscr{M}_{\mathscr{I}}}
and
\mathscr{M}_{\boldsymbol{j}^{*}_{\mathsf{K}}}\circ\mathscr{M}_{i_{\mathscr{G}_{\mathsf{K}}}}
were
equal on this nose. This in turn implied that for every map

\diamond_{\mathscr{I}}
\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mathrm{bool}^{*}\boldsymbol{\uptau}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle\mathrm{bool}^{*}\boldsymbol{\uptau}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mathrm{bool}^{*}\boldsymbol{\uptau}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{bool}^{*}\boldsymbol{\uptau}$}\mathclose{}{)}}_{\mathscr{I}}
f
, there existed a map

\diamond_{\mathscr{G}_{\mathsf{K}}}
\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle\mathrm{bool}^{*}\boldsymbol{\uptau}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle\mathrm{bool}^{*}\boldsymbol{\uptau}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mathrm{bool}^{*}\boldsymbol{\uptau}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{bool}^{*}\boldsymbol{\uptau}$}\mathclose{}{)}}_{\mathscr{G}_{\mathsf{K}}}
\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{\llbracket}\hbox{$\displaystyle f$}\mathclose{}{\rrbracket}}{\mathopen{}{\llbracket}\hbox{$\textstyle f$}\mathclose{}{\rrbracket}}{\mathopen{}{\llbracket}\hbox{$\scriptstyle f$}\mathclose{}{\rrbracket}}{\mathopen{}{\llbracket}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle f$}\mathclose{}{\rrbracket}}

such that
\boldsymbol{j}^{*}_{\mathsf{K}}{\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{\llbracket}\hbox{$\displaystyle f$}\mathclose{}{\rrbracket}}{\mathopen{}{\llbracket}\hbox{$\textstyle f$}\mathclose{}{\rrbracket}}{\mathopen{}{\llbracket}\hbox{$\scriptstyle f$}\mathclose{}{\rrbracket}}{\mathopen{}{\llbracket}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle f$}\mathclose{}{\rrbracket}}}=f
. Canonicity followed more-or-less
immediately by inspection of
\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{\llbracket}\hbox{$\displaystyle f$}\mathclose{}{\rrbracket}}{\mathopen{}{\llbracket}\hbox{$\textstyle f$}\mathclose{}{\rrbracket}}{\mathopen{}{\llbracket}\hbox{$\scriptstyle f$}\mathclose{}{\rrbracket}}{\mathopen{}{\llbracket}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle f$}\mathclose{}{\rrbracket}}
.

In this work, we have used a weaker notion of morphism and as a consequence,
\mathscr{M}_{\mathscr{I}}
is merely

bi
-initial. Accordingly, we cannot immediately conclude that
f
is in the image of

\mathscr{M}_{\boldsymbol{j}^{*}_{\mathsf{K}}}
. In fact, while it is not generally the case that

f=f_{\boldsymbol{j}^{*}_{\mathsf{K}}\circ i_{\mathscr{G}_{\mathsf{K}}}}
, it is possible to
realign

x_{i_{\mathscr{G}_{\mathsf{K}}}}
to an isomorphic arrow which does lie strictly over
f
.

Proof 7.2
.

First we note that
i_{\mathscr{G}_{\mathsf{K}}}{x}
lies over
\boldsymbol{j}^{*}_{\mathsf{K}}{i_{\mathscr{G}_{\mathsf{K}}}{x}}

by definition. Moreover, because

\mathscr{G}_{\mathsf{K}}
\mathscr{C}
\boldsymbol{j}^{*}_{\mathsf{K}}
is a fibration, we may construct a cartesian lift
of
\Gamma
\boldsymbol{j}^{*}_{\mathsf{K}}{i_{\mathscr{G}_{\mathsf{K}}}{\Gamma}}
\boldsymbol{\iota}
. Diagrammatically, there exists
two squares:

\boldsymbol{\iota}^{*}{i_{\mathscr{G}_{\mathsf{K}}}{\Gamma}}
\Gamma
i_{\mathscr{G}_{\mathsf{K}}}{\Gamma}
\boldsymbol{j}^{*}_{\mathsf{K}}{i_{\mathscr{G}_{\mathsf{K}}}{\Gamma}}
\boldsymbol{\iota}^{\dagger}
\boldsymbol{\iota}

\mathsf{y}_{\mathscr{G}_{\mathsf{K}}}{i_{\mathscr{G}_{\mathsf{K}}}(\Gamma)}
\mathsf{y}_{\mathscr{I}}{\boldsymbol{j}^{*}_{\mathsf{K}}{i_{\mathscr{G}_{\mathsf{K}}}{\Gamma}}}
X_{\mathscr{G}_{\mathsf{K}}}
X_{\mathscr{I}}
i_{\mathscr{G}_{\mathsf{K}}}{x}
\boldsymbol{j}^{*}_{\mathsf{K}}{i_{\mathscr{G}_{\mathsf{K}}}{x}}

Observe that
\boldsymbol{\iota}^{\dagger}
is an isomorphism because it is cartesian over an isomorphism.
Unfolding the definition of a 2-morphism, we see that

\boldsymbol{j}^{*}_{\mathsf{K}}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle i_{\mathscr{G}_{\mathsf{K}}}{x}\circ\mathsf{y}_{\mathscr{G}_{\mathsf{K}}}{\boldsymbol{\iota}}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle i_{\mathscr{G}_{\mathsf{K}}}{x}\circ\mathsf{y}_{\mathscr{G}_{\mathsf{K}}}{\boldsymbol{\iota}}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle i_{\mathscr{G}_{\mathsf{K}}}{x}\circ\mathsf{y}_{\mathscr{G}_{\mathsf{K}}}{\boldsymbol{\iota}}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle i_{\mathscr{G}_{\mathsf{K}}}{x}\circ\mathsf{y}_{\mathscr{G}_{\mathsf{K}}}{\boldsymbol{\iota}}$}\mathclose{}{)}}=x
. Accordingly, we may
paste together these two diagrams to obtain the following:

\mathsf{y}_{\mathscr{G}_{\mathsf{K}}}{\boldsymbol{\iota}^{*}{i_{\mathscr{G}_{\mathsf{K}}}{\Gamma}}}
\mathsf{y}_{\mathscr{I}}{\Gamma}
X_{\mathscr{G}_{\mathsf{K}}}
X_{\mathscr{I}}
i_{\mathscr{G}_{\mathsf{K}}}{x}\circ\mathsf{y}_{\mathscr{G}_{\mathsf{K}}}{\boldsymbol{\iota}^{\dagger}}
\boldsymbol{j}^{*}_{\mathsf{K}}\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\displaystyle i_{\mathscr{G}_{\mathsf{K}}}{x}\circ\mathsf{y}_{\mathscr{G}_{\mathsf{K}}}{\boldsymbol{\iota}}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\textstyle i_{\mathscr{G}_{\mathsf{K}}}{x}\circ\mathsf{y}_{\mathscr{G}_{\mathsf{K}}}{\boldsymbol{\iota}}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptstyle i_{\mathscr{G}_{\mathsf{K}}}{x}\circ\mathsf{y}_{\mathscr{G}_{\mathsf{K}}}{\boldsymbol{\iota}}$}\mathclose{}{)}}{\mathopen{}{(}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle i_{\mathscr{G}_{\mathsf{K}}}{x}\circ\mathsf{y}_{\mathscr{G}_{\mathsf{K}}}{\boldsymbol{\iota}}$}\mathclose{}{)}}
x

Therefore,
\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{\llbracket}\hbox{$\displaystyle x$}\mathclose{}{\rrbracket}}{\mathopen{}{\llbracket}\hbox{$\textstyle x$}\mathclose{}{\rrbracket}}{\mathopen{}{\llbracket}\hbox{$\scriptstyle x$}\mathclose{}{\rrbracket}}{\mathopen{}{\llbracket}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle x$}\mathclose{}{\rrbracket}}\overset{\textit{def}}{=\joinrel=}i_{\mathscr{G}_{\mathsf{K}}}{x}\circ\mathsf{y}_{\mathscr{G}_{\mathsf{K}}}{\boldsymbol{\iota}^{\dagger}}
is a morphism lying
strictly over
x
. The final condition is immediate because

\mathchoice{\mathopen{}{\llbracket}\hbox{$\displaystyle\Gamma$}\mathclose{}{\rrbracket}}{\mathopen{}{\llbracket}\hbox{$\textstyle\Gamma$}\mathclose{}{\rrbracket}}{\mathopen{}{\llbracket}\hbox{$\scriptstyle\Gamma$}\mathclose{}{\rrbracket}}{\mathopen{}{\llbracket}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\Gamma$}\mathclose{}{\rrbracket}}\cong i_{\mathscr{G}_{\mathsf{K}}}(\Gamma)
by definition.

Remark 86
.

One might hope that Lemma
85
implies the existence of a morphism

\mathscr{M}_{\mathscr{I}}
\mathscr{M}_{\mathscr{G}_{\mathsf{K}}}
\mathscr{M}_{j}
which satisfies the identity

\mathscr{M}_{\boldsymbol{j}^{*}_{\mathsf{K}}}\circ\mathscr{M}_{j}=\mathbf{id}_{\mathscr{I}}
on the nose. Simply applying the realignment
procedure to every element of
\mathscr{M}_{\mathscr{I}}
does not result in a morphism, however, because it is
not functorial, merely pseudo-functorial. This should not be surprising: realignment relies on a
choice of cartesian lift, which is only pseudo-functorial in general.
∎
